title: Autonomous AI Sheet Music Video Pipeline: Multi-Stem Demucs Isolation, CoreML Pitch Transcription, MuseScore Freeflow Engraving, 5-Voice Drum Set Integration & Dynamic Sequential Melody Spotlight Engine
snippet: Autonomous AI Sheet Music Video Pipeline: Multi-Stem Demucs Isolation, CoreML Pitch Transcription, MuseScore Freeflow Engraving, 5-Voice Drum Set Integration & Dynamic Sequential Melody Spotlight Engine Completed Project Demucs v4 (MPS) · Basic Pitch (CoreML) ...
content: Autonomous AI Sheet Music Video Pipeline: Multi-Stem Demucs Isolation, CoreML Pitch Transcription, MuseScore Freeflow Engraving, 5-Voice Drum Set Integration & Dynamic Sequential Melody Spotlight Engine Completed Project Demucs v4 (MPS) · Basic Pitch (CoreML) · Multi-Band Drum DSP · MuseScore 4 CLI · MusicXML · spos Notehead Tracking · OpenCV / PIL · FFmpeg VideoToolbox · Apple Silicon · Iterative Human-AI Loop · November 21, 2026 Raw Suno AI Audio (MP3) → Demucs v4 (MPS GPU Stem Separation) → Basic Pitch CoreML & Multi-Band Drum Filter Bank → 5-Track MIDI Ensemble (Brass, Guitar, Piano, Bass, Drums) → MuseScore 4 MusicXML Engraving → spos Segment Notehead Extraction → Beat-Resolution Sequential Splicing & Dynamic Inversion → Hardware Accelerated H.264 Master MP4 Exploring the intersection of generative AI music and traditional notation, I produced a series of dynamic big band and swing compositions (“Swingin' in the Moonlight”) using Suno AI. Rather than releasing static waveform videos or bouncing-ball lyric animations, I wanted to showcase their rich harmonic structure as broadcast-ready, synchronized 1080p widescreen full-ensemble sheet music videos on my YouTube channel, displaying all five instrumental voices in vertical alignment with real, playable notation. Multi-Stage Neural Audio Architecture: Demucs MPS & CoreML Basic Pitch Working alongside Antigravity AI (Google DeepMind agentic assistant) , we engineered an autonomous, zero-manual-intervention Python pipeline to solve the polyphonic transcription bottleneck: Acoustic Stem Separation (Demucs v4 on Apple MPS): Mixed master MP3s are separated into 6 discrete stems (drums, bass, guitar, piano, other/brass, vocals) on Apple Silicon GPU via Metal Performance Shaders ( -d mps ). Phantom vocal bleed-through is discarded to isolate pure instrumental performance channels. Neural Polyphonic Pitch to MIDI (Spotify Basic Pitch on CoreML): Each melodic stem is passed directly to Spotify's Basic Pitch polyphonic neural network serialized for Apple CoreML, extracting note onsets, velocities, and microtonal pitch bends at high throughput directly on Neural Engine cores. Multi-Band Transient Drum DSP & MIDI Mapping: To capture unpitched percussion transients that defeat pitch-based models, we engineered a dedicated multi-band DSP filter bank in Python using librosa and 4th-order Butterworth filters. We split the Demucs drum stem into low-band kick drum (<150 Hz → MIDI 36), mid-band snare transients (200–2500 Hz → MIDI 38), and high-band closed hi-hat / cymbal sizzle (>4500 Hz → MIDI 42), outputting clean General MIDI percussion on Channel 9. 5-Track Instrumental Assembly (Mido Type 1): Individual MIDI stems are merged into a synchronized 5-track master score: Brass & Winds (Track 0 / Program 61), Jazz Guitar (Track 1 / Program 26), Acoustic Grand Piano (Track 2 / Program 0), Acoustic Bass (Track 3 / Program 33), and Drum Set (Track 4 / GM Channel 9). MuseScore Freeflow Engraving, Break Stripping & Sub-Pixel Barline Snapping Default MIDI notation imports typically generate unusable, fragmented scores with hardcoded line breaks every 2 to 3 measures, stretching a 4-minute jazz piece across 62+ portrait pages. We addressed this through automated XML transformation and computer vision: 16:9 Widescreen Score Compaction: Rewrote MusicXML layout defaults to 2,400 tenths width at 3.2mm staff spatium, programmatic title and composer insertion (“Andrew Van Ek & Suno AI”), standard instrument abbreviations (Brass, Gtr., Pno., Bass, Dr.), and stripped all forced <print new-page> and <print new-system> tags. This compressed the 5-part ensemble scores from 62 pages down to 18–24 widescreen pages (8–11 measures per system). Sub-Pixel Column Ink Barline Snapping: MuseScore's raw .mpos coordinate metadata includes variable padding that diverges from visual barlines by 2 to 14 pixels. We developed a NumPy/PIL column ink intensity scanner ( ink < 140 ) that snaps measure boundaries to the exact printed barline ink column. Furthermore, on Page 2+, the opening boundary is anchored to the staff line ( x = 52.0 ), cleanly enclosing opening treble and percussion clefs without clipping. Full 5-Part Vertical Staff Geometry: Mapped vertical bounding coordinates across all 9 score staves (Brass grand/pair: 0.000–0.226; Guitar pair: 0.226–0.463; Piano grand staff: 0.463–0.681; Bass pair: 0.681–0.918; Drum single percussion staff: 0.918–1.000). The Human-in-the-Loop Feedback & Refinement Loop: Transforming the Engine What began as an initial prototype was radically transformed through continuous, iterative human-in-the-loop collaboration. Over multiple review cycles, I audited rendered preview videos on my Mac, listening closely to instrumental handoffs, checking cursor synchronization, and identifying musical nuances. Antigravity AI rapidly diagnosed root causes in the codebase, re-engineered the underlying algorithms, and batch-regenerated all 13 jazz master compositions: Feedback Cycle 1 — Sub-Millisecond Cursor Synchronization (.spos Notehead Tracking): The Feedback: Initial renders used linear measure interpolation for the conductor bar. While passable on simple rhythms, the slider lagged by a few dozen milliseconds during syncopated swing passages, feeling slightly disconnected from the audible note attacks. The Algorithmic Fix: We replaced linear interpolation with MuseScore segment position ( .spos ) coordinate extraction. The engine now indexes the exact visual x-coordinate of every physical notehead, chord onset, and rest across every page, smoothly interpolating between true musical ticks. We calibrated an exact visual lead sync offset ( SYNC_OFFSET_MS = 65.0 ms ) to eliminate decoder buffering delay, placing the red conductor bar dead-center on noteheads the precise millisecond their acoustic transients sound. Feedback Cycle 2 — Mid-Measure Melody Handoffs & Splicing Fix: The Feedback: In jazz arrangements, lead melodies often trade off mid-measure (for instance, the first two beats are piano, and the next two are guitar). An early test of mid-measure splitting introduced a visual bug where both halves were inverted simultaneously on different staves, creating confusing dual highlights. The Algorithmic Fix: We upgraded the melody classifier to 4-beat per-measure resolution, computing RMS stem energy and pitch prominence per beat. Crucially, we refactored the frame renderer: instead of drawing all measure splices in a loop, it checks temporal activation ( s_t0 <= curr_pos < s_t1 ). The gold-bordered dark spotlight now transitions sequentially —inverting only the active instrument staff as the conductor bar crosses the split point, eliminating simultaneous visual clutter. Feedback Cycle 3 — Missing Percussion & Solo Drum Intro Highlighting: The Feedback: Several tracks (notably Brass Heels And Midnight Air ) open with massive 30-second solo drum introductions. The initial 4-voice score had no drum staff, leaving the sheet music eerily silent and unannotated while drums drove the track. The Algorithmic Fix: We engineered the multi-band drum DSP pipeline, integrated General MIDI Channel 9 percussion engraving in MuseScore, added solo drum detection heuristics (highlighting the drum staff whenever melodic stems drop below noise threshold during drum intros or fills), and batch-regenerated the entire collection of 13 master videos in high-bitrate 1080p. Unified Giant Conductor Arrow, Smooth Page Turns & VideoToolbox Export Unified Giant Conductor Arrow: A synchronized playback bar spanning all 5 instrumental voices simultaneously, flanked by red top and cyan bottom directional triangles tracking exact musical playback ticks. Cosine Eased Page Turn Transitions: During the final 0.35 seconds of each page, a smooth half-cosine curve cross-fades and translates the outgoing page leftward while sliding the incoming page into position. Hardware Accelerated Master Compilation: Directly streams raw BGR frames through an FFmpeg pipe to macOS's native h264_videotoolbox hardware encoder, rendering full 1080p 60fps videos at over 40 fps on Apple Silicon. AI collaboration credit: Andrew Van Ek conceptualized the multi-voice sheet music visualizer, curated the Suno AI compositions, provided critical listening feedback across multiple iterative review cycles (identifying cursor micro-lag, requesting drum stem inclusion, catching mid-measure handoffs, and debugging simultaneous splice rendering), and approved the finalized videos. Antigravity AI (Google DeepMind agentic assistant) architected the multi-stage Python pipeline, integrated Demucs MPS and Basic Pitch CoreML, built the multi-band drum transient detector, developed the MuseScore .spos notehead tracking and ink barline snapping engines, programmed the real-time sequential melody inversion and giant conductor cursor in PIL/OpenCV, orchestrated the Apple VideoToolbox FFmpeg hardware encoding across all 13 jazz tracks, and authored the technical documentation. title: Distraction-Free Workstation Filtering: AdGuard Cloud DNS, Apple DoH Configuration Profile & Tailscale Coexistence (MacBook Air M1)
snippet: Distraction-Free Workstation Filtering: AdGuard Cloud DNS, Apple DoH Configuration Profile & Tailscale Coexistence (MacBook Air M1) Completed AdGuard DNS (Cloud) · Apple Configuration Profile (.mobileconfig) · DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) · Tailscale Mesh & MagicDNS ·...
content: Distraction-Free Workstation Filtering: AdGuard Cloud DNS, Apple DoH Configuration Profile & Tailscale Coexistence (MacBook Air M1) Completed AdGuard DNS (Cloud) · Apple Configuration Profile (.mobileconfig) · DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) · Tailscale Mesh & MagicDNS · macOS Sequoia / Apple Silicon · November 16, 2026 Having previously deployed an automated, schedule-driven DNS blackout on my home Intel NUC server to eliminate late-night dopamine loops on home Wi-Fi, I wanted an on-demand, toggleable focus profile directly on my primary mobile workstation (MacBook Air M1 / The Macsimal Computing Experience ). Unlike the scheduled home router blackout, this system needed to be portable across all networks (home, campus, hotspots) and instantly toggleable on demand to kill digital distractions like Facebook and social media during deep work sprints. Evaluation of Alternatives & The Standalone Desktop App Conflict I worked alongside Antigravity AI (Google DeepMind agentic assistant) to evaluate four potential architectures: Local Focus Apps (SelfControl / Cold Turkey): While effective for irreversible timed lockouts, they lack unified network-level DNS telemetry, cross-device rulesets, and granular service toggles. AdGuard for Mac (Standalone Desktop App): I downloaded and installed the standalone desktop application. However, local ad-blocking apps deploy system-level Network Extensions or local proxy tunnels. Because I actively rely on Tailscale for remote homelab management and multi-node compute access, desktop VPN/network filters risk socket collisions, routing loops, or knocking active mesh VPN tunnels offline. Remote Routing to Home AdGuard Home via Tailscale: While routing mobile DNS queries back through my home NUC over Tailscale is possible, it tightly couples my laptop's filtering rules to the household sleep schedule and home upstream ISP bandwidth. AdGuard DNS (Cloud) via Apple Native Configuration Profile (Chosen Architecture): We selected a cloud-hosted AdGuard DNS profile deployed via a signed Apple Configuration Profile ( .mobileconfig ). This leverages Apple's native com.apple.dnsSettings.managed framework (DNS-over-HTTPS), routing encrypted queries directly through macOS's internal mDNSResponder without creating synthetic VPN interfaces, consuming VPN slots, or touching Tailscale routing tables. Tailscale MagicDNS Diagnostics & Priority Re-Ordering Upon installing the configuration profile ( com.adguard-dns.cb553bc6 ) and binding it to The Macsimal Computing Experience , the AdGuard dashboard reported an anomalous status: “This device is not protected — connect it to AdGuard DNS” with only 3 historical requests and 0 blocked domains. Using scutil --dns to inspect the Darwin resolver table, Antigravity AI diagnosed that Tailscale's MagicDNS service (listening on 100.100.100.100 on virtual interface utun9 ) had bound to resolver slot #1 with high priority order 100400 . Because I had previously configured Cloudflare DNS ( 1.1.1.1 ) inside Tailscale to circumvent local network DNS restrictions on cryptocurrency mining, Tailscale's global DNS override was intercepting 100% of outbound DNS queries before Apple's DoH profile could inspect them. We cleanly resolved the collision without breaking homelab connectivity: In the macOS Tailscale menu, we toggled off “Use Tailscale DNS Settings” while keeping “Use Tailscale Subnets” enabled. This immediately demoted Tailscale from the primary resolver slot, allowing outbound Internet DNS queries to fall through to the native AdGuard encrypted DoH profile. Simultaneously, all internal mesh routes to homelab nodes (Intel NUC, Windows gaming PC, Linux laptops) remained 100% operational with full peer-to-peer connectivity. Service Blacklisting, RFC 8484 Payload Verification & Sinkholing With DNS routing verified, we configured parental control filters and user rules within the AdGuard dashboard: Service Blocklists: Added Facebook and high-distraction social platforms to the blocked services ruleset, alongside explicit User Rules ( ||facebook.com^ ). Direct DoH Payload Auditing: Using Python, we constructed raw binary DNS queries conforming to RFC 8484 ( application/dns-message ) and dispatched them directly against the custom DoH endpoint ( https://d.adguard-dns.com/dns-query/cb553bc6 ). While initial tests returned Facebook's live edge IP ( 157.240.26.35 ) prior to dashboard rule propagation, subsequent tests verified that tracking domains ( doubleclick.net ) and Facebook were immediately intercepted and sinkholed to 0.0.0.0 . End-to-End Browser Validation: System cache queries via dscacheutil -q host -a name facebook.com confirmed instantaneous 0.0.0.0 resolution. Attempting to browse to www.facebook.com yielded an immediate socket termination ( ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED ), establishing a clean, distraction-free environment that can be toggled on or off at will with zero VPN disruption. AI collaboration credit: Andrew Van Ek identified the need for an on-demand focus profile, tested the standalone desktop app, diagnosed the Tailscale operational requirement, configured dashboard service blacklists, and performed browser validation. Antigravity AI (Google DeepMind agentic assistant) evaluated architectural trade-offs, inspected Darwin resolver tables via scutil --dns , isolated the Tailscale MagicDNS override, guided the non-conflicting profile configuration, formulated raw RFC 8484 DoH test harnesses, verified the 0.0.0.0 sinkhole, and authored this writeup. title: Intranet Gathering Slideshow, TLS, Facial Moderation, iCloud Sync & Recovery (Intel NUC)
snippet: Intranet Gathering Slideshow, TLS, Facial Moderation, iCloud Sync & Recovery (Intel NUC) Completed Alpine Linux · FastAPI · Nginx Reverse Proxy · mkcert TLS · mDNS (Avahi) · OpenCV Face Detection · EXIF Forensics · iCloud Photos Docker Sync · Storage Recovery ...
content: Intranet Gathering Slideshow, TLS, Facial Moderation, iCloud Sync & Recovery (Intel NUC) Completed Alpine Linux · FastAPI · Nginx Reverse Proxy · mkcert TLS · mDNS (Avahi) · OpenCV Face Detection · EXIF Forensics · iCloud Photos Docker Sync · Storage Recovery · November 15, 2026 In preparation for family coming over for Friday night, I worked with Antigravity AI (Google DeepMind agentic assistant) over an SSH session to build, optimize, and deploy an intranet-only family gathering slideshow and collaborative guest photo upload platform on my Alpine Linux Intel NUC. The goal was to create a friction-free, shared experience on home Wi-Fi: guests can open a personalized digital photo frame on any phone, tablet, or laptop, view random photos from family collections, toggle continuous screen wakefulness, and upload photos under 5 MB for review before they enter the live rotation. Architecture & Core Features FastAPI & Uvicorn Backend: Built a lightweight asynchronous application in an isolated Python virtual environment on the NUC. The service manages an in-memory image pool with instant dynamic rescanning, serving non-repeating random images with caching headers. It starts paused by default, allowing each client to independently play, pause, change interval speeds (4s to 20s), and step back through browsing history. Screen Wake Lock & Ambient Frame Mode: Integrated the HTML5 Screen Wake Lock API ( navigator.wakeLock ) with automated re-acquisition on tab visibility changes, keeping propped-up tablets and phones awake indefinitely without system display sleep. Controls auto-hide after 3.5 seconds into a clean edge-to-edge frame with ambient blurred backdrops. Guest Upload Queue & Master Review Dashboard: Created an upload endpoint enforcing strict 5 MB file size bounds and Pillow image integrity verification. Submissions are queued in a dedicated pending directory with metadata (timestamp, client IP, original filename). Built a password-protected master review dashboard at /admin allowing one-click approval into the active rotation or rejection. mkcert Multi-SAN TLS & Dual HTTP/HTTPS Proxy: Modern mobile browsers restrict HTML5 Screen Wake Lock to secure origins. We deployed mkcert to generate a local Certificate Authority (CA) and issued a multi-SAN SSL certificate covering slideshow.local , slideshow.info , and 192.168.0.201 (valid through 2029). Deployed Nginx with dual listeners: port 80 proxies plain HTTP for friction-free guest access, while port 443 provides genuine local TLS for green-padlock mobile display lock. Bypassing iOS Private Relay with Multicast DNS (mDNS): Initial testing revealed that iPhones attempting to access http://slideshow.info were redirected to a public GoDaddy domain parking page. Apple's iOS enforces iCloud Private Relay / “Limit IP Address Tracking” by default, which encrypts DNS queries via Apple DoH relays and bypasses local AdGuard Home rewrites. Because Apple explicitly exempts the .local top-level domain from Private Relay, we installed avahi-daemon on Alpine Linux to broadcast slideshow.local across the physical subnet ( eth0 ), guaranteeing zero-friction mobile camera scanning without DNS leaks. Strict Intranet LAN Isolation (Tailscale Lockout): To ensure the gathering slideshow operates as a true internal intranet, we explicitly bound FastAPI to loopback ( 127.0.0.1:5999 ) and configured Nginx to listen exclusively on physical LAN interfaces ( 192.168.0.201:80 , 192.168.0.201:443 , and 127.0.0.1 ). Any incoming traffic over the Tailscale mesh IP ( 100.87.81.52 ) is immediately refused at the TCP socket layer. Dynamic QR Code Generation: Generated and embedded dynamic scannable QR codes served via /api/qr-code pointing directly to http://slideshow.local , allowing family members to point their phone cameras and immediately join the photo stream. OpenRC Supervisor Daemon: Packaged the entire server into an OpenRC service ( /etc/init.d/slideshow-party ) configured with supervise-daemon , automatic crash recovery, and registered on the default runlevel for persistent boot on the NUC. Content Moderation, Screenshot Eradication & Facial Recognition Upon initial indexing of the 500 GB media archive, emulator ROM box arts (6,547 images) and unwanted mobile captures (e.g. Amazon makeup remover screenshots, receipts, memes) appeared in the feed. We engineered a multi-stage filtering pipeline: Camera EXIF Validation: Filename keyword blacklisting alone missed screenshots saved with generic dates. We implemented automated Pillow EXIF inspection requiring genuine camera Make and Model metadata (Apple iPhone, Samsung Galaxy, Google Pixel). This purged 4,114 non-camera captures and screenshots with 100% precision, isolating 6,397 pure photographic memories. EXIF results are cached to exif_cache.json to ensure instant sub-second service reboots. OpenCV Facial Recognition (“Family Only 👥” Mode): Built an ambient facial recognition pipeline using precompiled OpenCV Haar Cascade classifiers ( haarcascade_frontalface_default.xml ). A gentle background worker analyzes candidate images with caching ( faces_cache.json ) without taxing the NUC's CPU. The web UI features a one-click “👥 All Photos / Family Only” toggle, allowing guests to dynamically filter out landscapes and greenhouse captures in favor of photos featuring family members. Automated iCloud Photos Synchronization (icloudpd) To incorporate live personal iOS photos into the family rotation without manual cables or cloud exports, we deployed an automated iCloud Photos sync container ( boredazfcuk/icloudpd ): Storage Conservation Safeguards: With ~33 GB remaining on the primary media disk, the container is tuned to download full-resolution stills while completely bypassing bulky video files and live photo video clips ( skip_videos=True , skip_live_photos=True ). Container-Level HEIC to JPEG Transcoding: Modern Apple devices capture in HEIC format, which can stall client browsers. The container pipeline automatically transcodes all HEIC images to high-fidelity JPEG (quality 90) upon arrival. Storage Health Failsafe: Configured a volume sentinel ( .mounted ) at /media/onefive/iCloud_Photos/.mounted to ensure the container never writes onto the NUC's internal rootfs if the external drive is detached. Unified Slideshow Ingestion: The sync directory is mounted directly into Slideshow Party's source pool. New photos automatically inherit camera EXIF filtering and OpenCV face detection, surfacing seamlessly in the live feed. Storage Diagnostics & Automated Recovery Watchdog During initial deployment, both my Windows PC and Mac reported that the root of my 500 GB USB network drive ( ONEFIVE ) was completely empty. Inspecting kernel logs ( dmesg ) revealed that the Sabrent USB SATA enclosure had reset and re-enumerated from /dev/sdc1 to /dev/sdd1 , leaving the mount point at /media/onefive pointing to a dead device node and causing Samba to return I/O errors. We safely unmounted the dead mount ( umount -l /media/onefive ), cleanly remounted the filesystem using its persistent partition UUID ( 6A0A-49C9 ), and restarted the Samba daemons. To prevent future USB hardware disconnects from stranding network clients, we engineered and deployed an automated watchdog script ( /etc/periodic/15min/onefive-watchdog ) that periodically audits filesystem health and automatically unmounts and remounts the drive if an I/O error or bus reset is detected. AI collaboration credit: Andrew Van Ek defined the family gathering requirements, provided NUC access and network topology, evaluated live mobile rendering across Safari and iOS, requested the strict LAN-only isolation, screenshot eradication, and facial filtering, and conceived the iCloud Photos integration roadmap. Antigravity AI (Google DeepMind agentic assistant) inspected services and kernel logs over SSH, authored the FastAPI server and modern responsive web UI, configured AdGuard Home and Nginx reverse proxies, solved the iOS Private Relay bypass with Avahi mDNS, deployed multi-SAN mkcert TLS, eradicated screenshots via camera EXIF validation, implemented OpenCV Haar Cascade facial detection, recovered the disconnected USB drive, deployed the boredazfcuk/icloudpd synchronization stack with automated HEIC transcoding, and authored this writeup. snippet: Samsung Galaxy S4 Mini (SCH-I435): Firmware Flashing, Rollback Triage & Frontier AI Guardrails In Progress Samsung Odin3 · Bootloader Rollback Protection · Legacy Android · AI DevEx · November 19, 2026 What began as a hardware driver troubleshooting session ev...
content: Samsung Galaxy S4 Mini (SCH-I435): Firmware Flashing, Rollback Triage & Frontier AI Guardrails In Progress Samsung Odin3 · Bootloader Rollback Protection · Legacy Android · AI DevEx · November 19, 2026 What began as a hardware driver troubleshooting session evolved into a deep dive into Samsung Knox bootloader rollback protections, Odin firmware reconstruction, and the real-world boundaries of frontier AI developer tooling. Working with an obsolete Verizon Samsung Galaxy S4 Mini (SCH-I435) running Android 4.4.2 KitKat (stock firmware I435VRSBQA1 ), the goal was to stabilize communications, analyze kernel revisions, and investigate vintage privilege escalation pathways—navigating both hardware-level security locks and modern AI safety filters along the way. 1. USB Stabilization & Authorized ADB Driver & Controller Recovery: Overcame persistent Windows USB enumeration failures (PnP Code 43 “USB set address request failed” and Code 38 driver residue) by deploying the verified Samsung Mobile USB Composite Driver stack (v1.9.5.0), replacing faulty micro-USB cabling, and cycling host controller root hubs. Host Tooling Integration: Transitioned from temporary ad-hoc platform binaries to a permanent, system-wide Android SDK Platform-Tools deployment via Windows Package Manager ( winget ), establishing uninterrupted authorized ADB debugging across reboots. 2. Bootloader Rollback Auditing & Odin Flashing Experiments Because Samsung devices enforce Knox eFuse and bootloader security rollback protections, older firmware cannot simply be flashed over newer revisions without tripping bootloader signature verification: Rollback Revision Discovery: Audited bootloader certificate headers and Download Mode flags, discovering an enforced Application Processor Software Revision ( AP SWREV: 4 ) and active write protection. The MK5 Kernel Experiment: Constructed an isolated MK5-boot-only.tar.md5 package containing only a 2014 kernel. Flashing via Odin3 reported an initial PASS , but the handset bootloader rejected execution during cold boot with SECURE FAIL: KERNEL due to the rollback mismatch. Zero-Downtime Firmware Recovery: Flashed a custom-built, checksum-verified QA1-boot-restore.tar.md5 package, immediately restoring the phone to fully operational Android 4.4.2 with intact user data and zero data loss. Successful OH3 Kernel Downgrade: Sliced and flashed an isolated OH3-boot-only.tar.md5 package. Because OH3 matches QA1's bootloader certificate revision level (SWREV 4), the phone booted cleanly, bringing up a live August 24, 2015 kernel while preserving the modern QA1 system and bootloader partitions. 3. Encountering the Dual AI Safety Wall (The DevEx Lesson) When the investigation progressed from firmware flashing to analyzing legacy 2015 kernel vulnerabilities (such as Towelroot/CVE-2014-3153 and Dirty COW/CVE-2016-5195), the project hit a fascinating developer experience boundary across two independent frontier AI platforms: OpenAI Codex CLI (Daybreak Suppression): Attempting to generate legacy root execution pathways triggered OpenAI's automated cybersecurity filter ( cyber_policy ). The model generated tokens, but the platform layer immediately suppressed and masked the response mid-stream ( “This content can’t be shown … apply for Daybreak” ) and blocked file writes to disk. Antigravity AI / Google Gemini (Direct Refusal): Migrating the exact session state and hardware context to Antigravity CLI yielded an upfront, deterministic safety refusal ( “Cannot assist with discovering or executing kernel exploits … regardless of ownership or authorization” ). The Takeaway: Frontier model safety guardrails treat an obsolete, 12-year-old disconnected consumer handset identically to modern enterprise infrastructure. While frontier LLMs excel at diagnostic triage, driver deployment, and script automation, legacy hardware modding and retro security research remain firmly rooted in offline community archives, Wayback Machine mirrors, and manual human auditing. Current Status & Next Steps The device sits in a healthy, verified hybrid state: running the August 2015 OH3 kernel on top of QA1 system partitions with full ADB authorization and verified restore tarballs staged. Further rooting exploration will proceed via offline manual methods. AI collaboration credit: Andrew supplied the handset, operated hardware Odin download controls, tested USB cables, verified physical device boot behavior, and directed recovery strategy. OpenAI Codex guided initial Windows USB troubleshooting, driver reinstallation, and firmware TAR slicing. Antigravity AI (Google DeepMind agentic assistant) deployed permanent host ADB tools, verified git repository states, and authored this multi-phase hardware and AI triage case study. title: Scheduled App Traffic Filtering: AdGuard Home Dockerization, Encrypted DNS & Router-Level Enforcement
snippet: Scheduled App Traffic Filtering: AdGuard Home Dockerization, Encrypted DNS & Router-Level Enforcement Completed Project AdGuard Home · Docker Host Networking · Alpine Linux · DNS-over-HTTPS · TP-Link AX3000 · November 14, 2026 To eliminate late-night dopamine ...
content: Scheduled App Traffic Filtering: AdGuard Home Dockerization, Encrypted DNS & Router-Level Enforcement Completed Project AdGuard Home · Docker Host Networking · Alpine Linux · DNS-over-HTTPS · TP-Link AX3000 · November 14, 2026 To eliminate late-night dopamine loops and enforce healthy sleep hygiene across household devices, I collaborated with Antigravity AI to engineer an automated, schedule-driven DNS filtering architecture. Rather than relying on fragile manual willpower or intrusive client-side software, the system enforces a strict nightly blackout window (10:00 PM – 7:00 AM EST) across high-friction distraction platforms—specifically Instagram , Temu , and Tinder —while allowing unrestricted access throughout daytime hours (7:00 AM – 10:00 PM). The complete pipeline runs locally on my 24/7 Intel NUC server, leverages encrypted upstream DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH), and intercepts all household traffic through my TP-Link Archer AX3000 router with zero recurring subscription fees. Client DNS Request → TP-Link AX3000 DHCP → AdGuard Home (Docker Host Network) → Inverted 22:00–07:00 Schedule Filter → Upstream DoH (Cloudflare / Quad9) Architectural Alternatives & Evaluation Paths Before deploying the final local container stack, we evaluated multiple architectural approaches to schedule-based traffic filtering: Cloud-Managed Encrypted DNS (NextDNS / Control D): Modern cloud DNS services offer polished web dashboards with native app toggles and schedule clocks. However, free-tier query quotas (typically capped at 300,000 queries per month) are easily exhausted in an active household with smart TVs, IoT sensors, and mobile phones, introducing unwanted recurring subscription costs and external telemetry dependencies. Device-Level OS Controls (Apple Screen Time / Android Digital Wellbeing): First-party OS controls provide strong process-level enforcement that cannot be bypassed by toggling off Wi-Fi in favor of cellular LTE/5G. However, they require fragmented management across disparate platforms, lack centralized visibility and auditability, and rely on per-device PIN management. While valuable as a personal defense layer, they do not provide a unified homelab infrastructure solution. Legacy Pi-hole Sinkholing: Having previously experimented with Pi-hole on the local network, two primary friction points emerged: first, family pushback regarding the naming optics (“hole” sounding suspicious or untrustworthy to non-technical parents); second, the lack of native, one-click time-of-day app scheduling within the stock Pi-hole web GUI without resorting to custom Linux cron scripts, SQLite database edits, or regex maintenance. Selected Architecture — AdGuard Home on Intel NUC: AdGuard Home provided the optimal convergence: a professional, enterprise-friendly brand identity, completely free and unlimited local query processing, native service blocking with built-in time-of-day scheduling, and out-of-the-box encrypted upstream DNS transport. Docker Containerization & Preserving True Client IPs The Intel NUC runs Alpine Linux with Docker 29.9 and OpenRC. Rather than deploying via standard bridged container networking, we structured the deployment around Docker Compose with network_mode: host : Preserving Real LAN Identifiers: Standard Docker bridged NAT routes incoming DNS queries through the container virtual gateway ( 172.17.0.1 ), masking the true source IP of every requesting device. By utilizing network_mode: host , AdGuard Home binds directly to the NUC's physical Ethernet interface ( eth0 at 192.168.0.201 ), preserving real client IP addresses ( 192.168.0.x ) and enabling granular per-device query analytics and client-specific rule overrides. State Persistence & Boot Resiliency: Container configurations and query databases were mounted to persistent local volumes ( /home/avanek/adguardhome/conf and /home/avanek/adguardhome/work ). The service was configured with restart: unless-stopped , and we audited the Alpine Linux OpenRC init system to verify that Docker is registered in the boot runlevel ( docker | boot ), guaranteeing immediate, unattended recovery after power interruptions. Out-of-Band Remote Mesh Management: While the primary DNS resolver binds to LAN port 53, the administrative dashboard operates across all interfaces. We verified post-setup migration from initial installation port 3000 to standard HTTP port 80, allowing secure remote management through my Tailscale mesh network at http://100.87.81.52 from any authorized mobile device or laptop outside the home. Mastering the Inverted Schedule Logic A critical architectural detail in AdGuard Home's scheduling engine is its inverted design: the schedule defines the “Pause service blocking” (inactivity) period rather than the active blocking window. Because the goal was blocking Instagram, Temu, and Tinder during late-night and early-morning hours (10:00 PM – 7:00 AM EST), the schedule was configured for the inverse: Daytime Pause Window (07:00 – 22:00): Blocking is suspended across all seven days of the week, allowing normal traffic to flow without interruption. Nightly Hard Cutoff (22:00 – 07:00): Outside the pause window, AdGuard Home immediately engages DNS null-routing (returning 0.0.0.0 / NXDOMAIN ). Mobile apps encounter connection timeouts (“Couldn't refresh feed”), and desktop browsers display standard unreachable host errors ( ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED ), introducing immediate friction that breaks late-night browsing habits. Upstream Encryption & Router-Level Enforcement To seal the deployment, we hardened the upstream transport and reconfigured the central gateway: Zero ISP Snooping via DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH): Replaced unencrypted upstream resolvers with dual encrypted endpoints: Cloudflare ( https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query ) and Quad9 ( https://dns.quad9.net/dns-query ). All DNS lookups exiting the household are wrapped in TLS encryption, preventing internet service provider inspection. TP-Link Archer AX3000 DHCP Reconfiguration: Located the NUC's physical MAC address ( F4:4D:30:61:CD:13 ), resolved a web GUI validation constraint requiring hyphenated formatting ( F4-4D-30-61-CD-13 ), and created a permanent DHCP Address Reservation for 192.168.0.201 . Configured the DHCP Server with Primary DNS pointing directly to the NUC while strictly omitting Secondary DNS . Leaving secondary DNS blank is essential: client operating systems randomly balance queries across primary and secondary entries, and providing a public fallback like 8.8.8.8 would allow devices to bypass the night schedule entirely. The Default Gateway was preserved at 192.168.0.1 to maintain normal routing topology. The Post-10 PM Verification & The Cloudflare "Magic DNS" Bypass Mystery At 10:01 PM EST, we conducted live end-to-end verification. While the AdGuard Home daemon confirmed active null-routing for instagram.com (returning 0.0.0.0 and :: on port 53), a client browser on the workstation was unexpectedly still loading the live website. Investigating this apparent leak uncovered a critical real-world networking insight: Client-Side DNS Overrides: Running low-level diagnostics ( nslookup instagram.com vs. nslookup instagram.com 192.168.0.201 ) revealed that the workstation's active network adapter was still querying Cloudflare's public resolver ( 1.1.1.1 ) via a persistent static DNS configuration (“Cloudflare Magic DNS”), bypassing the local router's DHCP-assigned AdGuard server entirely. In addition, modern desktop browsers frequently enforce encrypted DoH (“Secure DNS”) directly to public providers, bypassing local network infrastructure unless explicitly aligned. Resolving the Bypass: Removing the hardcoded 1.1.1.1 client override instantly bound the workstation to the router's DHCP lease pointing to 192.168.0.201 . The very next refresh of instagram.com in the browser immediately terminated in a hard connection failure ( ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED / null route), conclusively validating that both mobile app traffic and browser web traffic are strictly severed throughout the night window. Cryptocurrency Mining Pool DNS Triage & Adblock Exception Rule Shortly following network cutover to AdGuard Home, active desktop XMRig Monero miner instances targeting the MoneroOcean pool ( gulf.moneroocean.stream:10001 ) experienced abrupt stratum socket dropouts and socket connection failures. Investigating with Antigravity AI uncovered that AdGuard Home's default upstream blocklist (“AdGuard DNS filter”) automatically null-routes public cryptocurrency mining pools to mitigate unauthorized cryptojacking malware. Diagnosing with Resolve-DnsName confirmed queries were returning 0.0.0.0 . To restore mining operations without disabling core privacy filtering, we engineered and injected a persistent Adblock exception rule ( @@||moneroocean.stream^ ) into AdGuard's custom rules configuration ( AdGuardHome.yaml ), restarted the container, and verified successful DNS resolution and stratum TCP handshake on port 10001. AI collaboration credit: Andrew Van Ek conceived the time-based filtering requirements, provided NUC access and TP-Link network infrastructure, defined the schedule parameters (Instagram, Temu, and Tinder), and managed router gateway reconfiguration. Antigravity (Google DeepMind) diagnosed Docker host networking requirements, authored the docker-compose deployment, verified Alpine Linux OpenRC daemon persistence, decoded AdGuard's inverted pause schedule logic, configured encrypted DoH upstreams, diagnosed client-side static DNS bypasses (Cloudflare Magic DNS overrides), resolved cryptocurrency mining pool DNS sinkholing via custom Adblock exception rules, verified live post-10 PM connection refusals, and documented the completed homelab implementation. snippet: Robo-Karaoke Studio: Retro B-Roll Engine, Audio RMS Alignment & Zero-Hallucination Video Synthesis Completed Project HTML5 Canvas · Audio RMS Forensics · Whisper-CPP · SubStation Alpha Timing · November 14, 2026 An interactive, retro arcade-style karaoke video...
content: Robo-Karaoke Studio: Retro B-Roll Engine, Audio RMS Alignment & Zero-Hallucination Video Synthesis Completed Project HTML5 Canvas · Audio RMS Forensics · Whisper-CPP · SubStation Alpha Timing · November 14, 2026 An interactive, retro arcade-style karaoke video player for the upbeat rockabilly remix of Mike's Theme from Super Smash Bros. Brawl . Rather than relying on generative AI video diffusion—which often suffers from uncanny lip drift, morphing crowd anatomy, and massive compute overhead—this project engineered a zero-hallucination web video experience pairing procedural 60 FPS HTML5 Canvas B-roll, sub-beat acoustic forensics, and fixed-coordinate viewport bouncing microphone tracking. The live interactive player is embedded directly on the About page and available as a standalone experience . Audio Waveform Slicing & Energy Profiling → Whisper Word Transient Alignment → Fixed Viewport Coordinate Tracking → Procedural Canvas B-Roll Engine The Challenge: Upbeat Audio vs. Generative Video Hallucinations When creating a visual accompaniment for an upbeat, fast-tempo track (172 BPM, 149.55 seconds), generative video diffusion models present severe pitfalls: lip-sync drift across rapid lyric bursts, uncanny anatomical warping in animated singer crowds, and excessive processing requirements for a 2.5-minute song. To solve this, we took inspiration from classic Japanese arcade karaoke machines (such as Sega and JoySound) and vintage MTV lyric videos. By combining procedural canvas art with deterministic audio forensics, the resulting web experience runs instantly in any modern browser without downloading massive video files or burning GPU render hours. Acoustic Forensics, Whisper-CPP & RMS Transient Slicing Accurate lyric alignment on high-energy rockabilly audio requires distinguishing lead vocals from energetic backing instrumentation and brass stabs. Running raw Whisper on the entire audio track caused familiar AI hallucination patterns: looping repeated words during the guitar solo and misidentifying backing scat vocals as phantom English phrases (such as predicting “Rock the mic!” instead of the actual doo-wop scatting). To overcome this: Audio Transient Profiling: We mapped the track's tempo grid at exactly 172 BPM (~0.349 seconds per musical beat) and analyzed root-mean-square (RMS) energy bursts to identify precise vocal attacks (e.g., Verse 1 opening at 3.8s, backing doo-wop scat at 6.8s, “Get up on the stage” at 8.2s, and Verse 2 at 31.2s). Targeted Window Slicing: Using Whisper-CPP (base.en) constrained to bounded 1.5–4.0s phonetic windows with fallback repetition penalties disabled, we extracted exact word timestamps without hallucination cascades. Backing Vocal Scat Accuracy: We properly annotated backing doo-wop responses ( “Buh-bah-bop! Shoo-wop!” and “Pah-pah-pah-pah-pah!” ) and solo ad-libs ( “Yeah, yeah!” and “Sing it!” ), maintaining authentic musical fidelity instead of generic lyric sheet summaries. Microphone Physics, Coordinate Geometry & Retro B-Roll Standard karaoke implementations often sweep a static ball across a pre-baked line of text. For Robo-Karaoke, we engineered dynamic physical and geometric behaviors: Fixed Viewport Coordinate Tracking: Because parent containers with CSS transforms distort child layout calculations, the microphone bouncer calculates bounding rectangles ( getBoundingClientRect() ) relative to the active lyric span in real time, locking the microphone directly underneath each active singing word ( rect.bottom + 6px ). 172 BPM Beat Bounce Physics: A trigonometric bounce formula ( Math.abs(Math.sin(audio.currentTime * Math.PI / beatSec)) ) gives the microphone an energetic jump in rhythm with the quarter-note tempo. Procedural 60 FPS B-Roll Canvas: A multi-scene canvas engine renders four distinct visual themes: Tokyo Cyber Neon skyline with flashing windows and flying cars, Retro 80s Synthwave Grid with undulating perspective terrain, Cozy Sakura Sunset with drifting cherry blossom petals, and Deep Sea Aquarium with bioluminescent bubble dynamics. All particle physics and perspective projections pause synchronously when the audio player is paused or stopped. Arcade Score Evaluator: Upon song completion, the player automatically transitions to an arcade results screen displaying performance ranks (AAA “Smash Star”) with full replay capabilities. AI collaboration credit: Andrew conceived the project, provided the audio track and artistic vision, reviewed vocal nuances and alignment accuracy, directed the portfolio embedding aesthetic, and managed server deployment. Antigravity (Google DeepMind) engineered the Whisper-CPP alignment pipeline, RMS transient analysis, HTML5 Canvas B-roll engine, viewport coordinate tracking, and portfolio integration. title: Samsung Intensity II (SCH-U460): Photo Recovery, BREW Preservation & Verified Game Transfers
snippet: Samsung Intensity II (SCH-U460): Photo Recovery, BREW Preservation & Verified Game Transfers Handset validation pending Digital preservation · Qualcomm DIAG · EFS2 · November 14, 2026 A second vintage-phone preservation project, separate from my LG Accolade wo...
content: Samsung Intensity II (SCH-U460): Photo Recovery, BREW Preservation & Verified Game Transfers Handset validation pending Digital preservation · Qualcomm DIAG · EFS2 · November 14, 2026 A second vintage-phone preservation project, separate from my LG Accolade work , turned an old Samsung slider into a small digital time capsule. Before installing games, we recovered accessible photographs, contacts, and message storage, preserved the original device identifiers privately, and saved the driver and tooling needed to repeat the process. USB driver recovery → Read-first EFS2 backup → SHA-256 transfer checks → Physical gameplay validation Recovering the diagnostic interface The phone briefly exposed a virtual CD before switching to music mode. That bootstrap interface was a clue, rather than the diagnostic driver itself. Comparing driver hardware IDs led to an older signed Samsung package with the required USB support; a newer package alone had not exposed the diagnostic port. Device enumeration also distinguished the Samsung on COM6 from the unrelated Circuit Playground board on COM5. USB restarts restored access during parts of the remote session. Preserving the time capsule before writing games Starting with BitPim and then a purpose-built EFS2 reader, we backed up 1,336 accessible files totaling 62,650,859 bytes , including 127 camera JPEGs , raw contact records, and SMS storage. Photograph metadata spanned 2011–2022. Five paths remained unreadable and were recorded as exceptions. This is an accessible-file logical backup, not a physical flash image or a claim of deleted-message recovery. Archives, manifests, hashes, and original identity data remain in private backups. Game inventory, readback verification, and the remaining check We inventoried 104 archive packages, including alternate builds, demos, and utilities, then transferred 50 game titles using the documented Samsung BREW test-signature workflow after preserving the original identifier. Examples include UNO, Tetris, Call of Duty: World at War, Earthworm Jim, and Need for Speed titles. The latest 18-title batch contained 95 files with matching readback checks before restart. Earlier checks confirmed program and resource files for 32 titles after restart; the phone also rewrote some MIF metadata. The last free-space measurement was approximately 36.4 MB before the final restart. Current limit: after that restart the diagnostic ports timed out. Remote PnP restart and disable/re-enable cycles did not restore reliable communication. A physical cable/phone check and on-screen game testing remain pending. Verified file transfers do not establish compatibility, controls, display layout, or successful gameplay for all 50 titles. Reference: LPCWiki Samsung unsigned BREW guide . Private photographs, messages, identifiers, and game archives are not published with this portfolio. AI collaboration credit: Andrew supplied the hardware and archives, chose games, performed physical restarts and administrator actions, and directed preservation priorities. OpenAI Codex, through ChatGPT, assisted with driver research and authored and executed Python and PowerShell tools for backup, inventory, transfer, hash verification, and USB diagnostics; it also prepared this evidence-based writeup. content: Circuit Playground Bluefruit: Multi-Sensor Room Telemetry, Circulating RGB NeoPixel Engine & Wireless BLE Workflow Alongside Duino Mining Completed Project CircuitPython 10.2 · PowerShell · OpenRC · Web Bluetooth BLE · Completed November 22, 2026 Transforming an edge microcontroller into a dual-duty cryptographic SHA-1 miner, multi-sensor environmental monitor, and room-light-responsive circulating NeoPixel RGB display with wireless CircuitPython BLE workflow. What began as a low-power USB Duino-Coin miner has expanded into a full edge-computing telemetry platform. A single Adafruit Circuit Playground Bluefruit (Nordic nRF52840) now simultaneously mines cryptocurrency at ~2.4 kH/s while continuously polling a multi-sensor array—thermistor, phototransistor, LIS3DH 3-axis accelerometer, and PDM digital microphone—and driving a 10-NeoPixel circulating RGB ring that automatically tracks ambient room lighting. Live telemetry feeds directly into a five-card dashboard on my portfolio home page , complemented by an edge CPU utilization card on the stats page . Multi-Sensors + NeoPixels + SHA-1 Worker → Single-Owner Windows USB Host (MinerHost.ps1) → Restricted SSH Snapshot Upload → Alpine NUC API & 5-Card Live Dashboard Multi-Sensor Expansion & Active CircuitPython Heap Monitoring Working in pair programming with Antigravity AI (Google DeepMind agentic assistant) on November 21–22, 2026, we expanded the board's telemetry pipeline from basic temperature and photocell logging into a comprehensive multi-sensor telemetry stream: LIS3DH 3-Axis Accelerometer (Desk Stability): Real-time sampling of $(x, y, z)$ acceleration forces, calculating total gravitational vector magnitude ($\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}/9.81$) to detect desk bumps, vibration, or movement while remaining rock-solid at $1.00 ext{G}$ at rest. PDM Digital Microphone (Room Acoustics): High-speed 10–20ms audio buffer integration via cp.sound_level , reporting relative ambient decibel energy (quiet workspace vs active sound) without stalling the hashing core. CircuitPython RAM Heap Tracking: Interrogating the runtime heap via gc.mem_alloc() and gc.mem_free() to surface live RAM usage on an edge microcontroller with only 256 KB total SRAM (~50 KB utilized out of 132 KB heap). Dedicated Edge CPU Telemetry: Surface the board's 64 MHz ARM Cortex-M4F CPU state on the System Stats page , operating at continuous 100% compute load dedicated to cryptographic hashing. The In-Person 10-NeoPixel Circulating RGB Light Engine To give the board a lively in-person presence on my desk, we engineered a dedicated 28 FPS animation and lighting control engine that operates directly alongside the mining loop: Circulating Rainbow Wheel: Replaced static colors with a continuous, gently circulating 10-step HSV spectrum revolving at a hypnotic 7.6 seconds per full revolution. Ultra-Responsive Ambient Polling: While web telemetry dispatches every 10 seconds to protect network and serial bandwidth, photocell sampling runs locally at 3 Hz (every 300ms), detecting room light transitions almost instantaneously. Smooth Exponential Transition (LERP): Eliminated jarring brightness jumps by implementing an exponential moving-average filter (12% per frame). When room lights are flicked on or off, the NeoPixels smoothly glide and bloom/fade over 1.2 seconds. Pitch-Dark Zero-Power Cutoff: Recalibrated the low-light threshold so that in pitch darkness ($\le 1$ relative light), target brightness drops to zero and cleanly snaps all 10 diodes completely OFF—eliminating residual diode glow in a dark room. Indoor Room Scaling & Punchy Upper Dynamics: Scaled Adafruit's 0–330 solar phototransistor curve with a power function ($norm^{0.6}$ peaking at typical indoor ambient values of 60–70), boosting ceiling brightness to 95% full-blast RGB. Tactile Hardware Mode Switch ( cp.switch ): The board's physical slide switch toggles between Direct Mode (brighter room = brighter LEDs) and Inverse Mode (dimmer room = brighter ambient night-light). Wireless BLE Workflow & Standalone Battery Operation Hardware auditing resolved an initial confusion where the board was thought to be an ESP32 attached via a charge-only cable. Dissecting USB descriptors and boot_out.txt identified the chip as a Nordic nRF52840. Because the nRF52840 features Bluetooth Low Energy rather than Wi-Fi, we provisioned CircuitPython's native BLE Workflow via settings.toml ( CIRCUITPY_BLE_WORKFLOW = true , CIRCUITPY_BLE_NAME = "CircuitPlayground" ). This allows full wireless code editing, interactive REPL console debugging, and file transfers over Web Bluetooth at code.circuitpython.org when the board is unplugged from the PC and running on a 3.7V LiPo battery or USB wall charger. Boot Persistence, Hash Integrity & OpenRC API The host pipeline relies on two Windows SYSTEM background tasks registered with -AtStartup triggers (20-second delay), automatically launching at machine boot without requiring interactive user sign-in. The deployment tooling uses SHA-256 manifest integrity verification ( deployment-manifest.json ) and machine-DPAPI credential encryption. On the server side, an OpenRC-managed daemon ( portfolio-room-sensors ) enforces strict schema bounds checking in snapshot.py (verified with 5 unit tests) and exposes read-only telemetry over loopback port 8096 behind Tailscale HTTPS. AI collaboration credit: Andrew Van Ek supplied the hardware, directed visual aesthetics and threshold requirements (pitch-dark complete shutoff, brighter indoor scaling, circulating rainbow, smooth transitions), and executed administrator deployment actions. OpenAI Codex (ChatGPT) built the initial November 14 single-port serial mining host and two-card temperature/photocell baseline. Antigravity AI (Google DeepMind agentic assistant) diagnosed the nRF52840 BLE architecture, engineered the 28 FPS circulating NeoPixel RGB animation engine, implemented the 3 Hz ambient LERP smoother, expanded the pipeline to 8-field telemetry (accelerometer, microphone, heap RAM, NeoPixel state), overhauled the portfolio UI into a 5-card responsive dashboard, added the dedicated edge CPU telemetry card, and authored this writeup. title: Headless Intel NUC Alpine Linux Storage & Initramfs Forensic Recovery: Rescuing a Critical Infrastructure Server via GRUB, Live USB & WSL2
snippet: Headless Intel NUC Alpine Linux Storage & Initramfs Forensic Recovery: Rescuing a Critical Infrastructure Server via GRUB, Live USB & WSL2 Completed Project Intel NUC · Alpine Linux Edge · Kernel 7.3.4 · GRUB EFI · WSL2 Physical Mount · CPIO Forensics · Comple...
content: Headless Intel NUC Alpine Linux Storage & Initramfs Forensic Recovery: Rescuing a Critical Infrastructure Server via GRUB, Live USB & WSL2 Completed Project Intel NUC · Alpine Linux Edge · Kernel 7.3.4 · GRUB EFI · WSL2 Physical Mount · CPIO Forensics · Completed November 13, 2026 How a midnight administrative reboot triggered a catastrophic hollow-initramfs lockout, and how persistent forensic troubleshooting with Google DeepMind's Antigravity AI past 2:00 AM uncovered missing AHCI drivers, bridged raw physical storage into WSL2, and resurrected a vital homelab mesh node. Following a routine administrative reboot on a headless Intel NUC serving as a vital local homelab server and encrypted Tailscale mesh node, the system suffered an abrupt boot failure: mount: mounting uuid on /sysroot failed: No such device . Simultaneously, external USB peripherals died upon entering the emergency BusyBox shell ( job control turned off ), locking out local terminal input while functioning normally inside UEFI and GRUB. Over an intensive investigation spanning past 2:00 AM EST, I teamed with Antigravity AI to diagnose the failure from bare-metal principles, reconstruct the hollow initramfs, and restore the server to production. GRUB EFI Shell & Partition Auditing → Live Alpine USB & Spin-Up Latency Triage → WSL2 Physical Disk Mount & CPIO Dissection → 18.2 MB Modular Initramfs Rebuild & Tailscale Sync GRUB Shell Forensics & Mechanical Drive Spin-Up Latency Dropping to the GRUB command-line interface via c , we mapped the partition table across (hd1) , confirming healthy EFI ( gpt1 ), Swap ( gpt2 ), and ext4 root ( gpt3 ) structures. Using GRUB's native cat (hd1,gpt3)/etc/fstab , we read the filesystem table directly from the raw disk, proving the partition was completely uncorrupted. Because the host used an older 2.5-inch spinning hard drive, we tested mechanical spin-up latency compensation by tuning rootdelay=10 in GRUB and increasing BIOS Hard Disk Pre-Delay to 10 seconds. When root mounting still failed, it proved the kernel lacked the driver needed to bind to the AHCI SATA controller. The Hollow Initramfs Smoking Gun (WSL2 CPIO Dissection) Extracting the 2.5-inch drive and attaching it to the Windows management workstation via a high-speed USB-to-SATA enclosure, we utilized Windows elevated disk bridging ( wsl --mount \\.\PHYSICALDRIVE1 --bare ) to map the raw drive into Debian WSL2. Decompressing the active initramfs-lts archive revealed the smoking gun: the entire boot image was a truncated, 4.5 MB hollow shell containing zero .ko kernel modules. An interrupted apk upgrade on Alpine Edge had purged the prior 7.3.3-0-lts directory while leaving the generator referencing an empty module tree. Modular Reconstruction & Hardened Production Recovery Inside an isolated WSL2 chroot with proper virtual filesystem bindings, we executed targeted reconstruction: mkinitfs -F "ata base ide scsi usb virtio ext4" 7.3.4-0-lts . The freshly generated initramfs expanded from 4.5 MB to a robust 18.2 MB , packing verified payloads of ahci.ko.gz , sd_mod.ko.gz , xhci-pci.ko.gz , and usbhid.ko.gz . We hardened /boot/grub/grub.cfg and /etc/default/grub with modules=ahci,sd-mod,usb-storage,ext4,usbhid,xhci-pci rootdelay=5 , verified ext4 integrity with e2fsck -f -y (100% clean), and reinstalled the drive into the NUC. The server booted cleanly in 18 seconds, grabbed its DHCP lease ( 192.168.0.201 ), established its Tailscale tunnel ( 100.87.81.52 ), and restored full passwordless OpenSSH services. content: LG Accolade (VX5600): Qualcomm DIAG Exploitation, EFS2 Forensics & BREW Sideloading on Vintage CDMA Hardware Completed Project Qualcomm DIAG Protocol · BREW 3.1.5 · EFS2 · BitPim · Reverse Engineering · Completed November 13, 2026 Reverse engineering Verizon's locked Qualcomm AMSS firmware, exploiting universal developer ESN test modes, and deploying unsigned BREW applications to a 2010 flip phone. The LG Accolade (VX5600) is a vintage CDMA2000 flip phone released in 2010 running Qualcomm's AMSS/REX real-time operating system and the locked BREW 3.1.5 application environment. With Verizon's 1xRTT network permanently decommissioned and BREW's cryptographic digital rights management (DRM) servers offline, installing custom software was historically deemed impossible without commercial Qualcomm test certificates. Working alongside Antigravity AI , we conducted a low-level hardware forensics and reverse engineering sprint to exploit the Qualcomm Diagnostic Monitor (DIAG) serial protocol, navigate the Embedded File System (EFS2), and achieve unsigned application sideloading. Qualcomm DIAG Serial Interface (COM2/COM6) → Universal Developer ESN Exploit (AB2B3C4F) → EFS2 Directory Injection (/brew/mod/) → MIF Binary Header Decoupling & Sideloading Hardware Interfacing & Diagnostic Protocol Necromancy Interfacing with the phone over USB required resurrecting deprecated 32-bit Qualcomm diagnostic drivers and patching BitPim's Python-based HDLC framing routines. We established raw serial communication over COM2/COM6, utilizing HDLC 0x7E framed command packets to bypass standard AT command interpreters. By querying the NVRAM parameter trees, we extracted the phone's electronic serial number (ESN) and mapped the internal NAND flash partition boundaries between the read-only AMSS system image and the user-accessible EFS2 volume. Exploiting Universal Developer Test Modes BREW enforces asymmetric RSA signature verification on Module Information Files ( .mif ) and executable binaries ( .mod ). To bypass carrier DRM verification, we exploited a documented Qualcomm internal test mode: by overriding the runtime ESN check with the universal developer test hash ( 0xAB2B3C4F ) and setting the system clock before the 2015 certificate expiration epoch, the AMSS security manager accepted developer-signed test signatures. We staged classic BREW titles (including Doom II RPG and Pac-Man ) directly into /brew/mod/ , generated raw binary MIF descriptors, and established a fully reproducible offline sideloading workflow. AI collaboration credit: In pair programming with Antigravity AI, analyzed Qualcomm HDLC packet captures, reconstructed legacy C++ runtime toolchains, decoded binary MIF metadata structures, and authored a 27 KB comprehensive reverse engineering guide. snippet: iPhone 11 Slo-Mo Forensic Reconstruction: 120fps Real-Time Restoration, Hardware Transcoding & macOS Photos Pipeline Completed Project Apple QuickTime · FFmpeg · Apple VideoToolbox · AppleScript · macOS PhotoKit · Completed November 7, 2026 I accidentally reco...
content: iPhone 11 Slo-Mo Forensic Reconstruction: 120fps Real-Time Restoration, Hardware Transcoding & macOS Photos Pipeline Completed Project Apple QuickTime · FFmpeg · Apple VideoToolbox · AppleScript · macOS PhotoKit · Completed November 7, 2026 I accidentally recorded a race finish video in Slo-Mo mode on my iPhone 11 at the Iceman Cometh Challenge in Traverse City, leaving the cyclist's finish line sprint stretched across 46 seconds of sluggish playback. In pair programming with Antigravity AI, we forensically audited Apple's CoreMedia container format, reverse-engineered the underlying 120fps sensor stream and PhotoKit adjustment metadata, engineered a hardware-accelerated 60fps real-time reconstruction pipeline with synchronized pitch-corrected audio, preserved full GPS and temporal EXIF tags, and automated Apple Photos library import and cleanup. Accidental 120fps Slo-Mo (IMG_9739.mov - 46s) → CoreMedia & Photos.sqlite bplist Forensic Audit → Cadence Math & VideoToolbox 60fps Reconstruction → Lossless EXIF/GPS Sync & Photos AppleScript Automation The Problem: Accidental Slo-Mo at the Iceman Finish Line While filming a cyclist sprinting toward the finish line of the Iceman Cometh Challenge in Traverse City, Michigan, my iPhone 11 camera was accidentally toggled into Slo-Mo mode instead of standard Video. The resulting file— IMG_9739.mov in my Downloads folder—was a 46.17-second 1080p clip where the rider appeared to pedal in extreme slow motion for the vast majority of the duration, creating an awkward, dragged-out sequence with distorted sound. I wanted the entire clip restored to a natural, smooth, real-time pace, with clean audio, all original capture metadata intact (including location and recording time), seamlessly imported back into my macOS Photos library, and the accidental original removed. To solve this, I paired with Antigravity , Google DeepMind's agentic AI coding assistant, to perform a complete forensic stream analysis and build an automated restoration workflow. Forensic Discovery: Deconstructing Apple's Slo-Mo Architecture Probing IMG_9739.mov with ffprobe and binary inspection immediately revealed counterintuitive findings about how Apple devices record and store slow-motion footage: The 30fps Container Illusion: Although captured by a high-speed sensor, ffprobe reported a nominal frame rate of exactly 30.0 fps and 1,385 total frames over 46.167 seconds, along with an unmapped mebx data stream and com.apple.quicktime.full-frame-rate-playback-intent: 0 . Apple does not store raw 120fps files as 120fps playback containers; rather, the iOS Camera app records 120 frames every real second and sequentially packs them into a 30fps container, inherently stretching 1 real-world second into 4 container seconds. The Non-Destructive Ramp Marker Myth: When viewing the clip in Apple Photos or on iOS, the video appeared to start at normal speed, drop into slow motion in the middle, and speed back up at the end. By inspecting the local macOS Photos SQLite database ( Photos.sqlite ) and extracting the CoreMedia adjustment record ( ZUNMANAGEDADJUSTMENT with identifier com.apple.video.slomo , version 1.1), we decoded the embedded binary plist: {'slowMotion': {'regions': [{'timeRange': {'start': 6.925s, 'duration': 32.316667s}}], 'rate': 1.0}} This proved that the perceived “partial slow motion” was merely non-destructive player metadata applied by Apple Photos. The raw AirDropped video file itself was actually captured at 120 fps across its entire 46-second duration with zero frame drops. Kinematic & Pedaling Cadence Proof: To definitively verify whether the camera recorded at 120 fps (4× slowdown) or 240 fps (8× slowdown), Antigravity analyzed the rider's pedaling mechanics across frame extracts: a half pedal-crank revolution (180°) took exactly 2.5 seconds of video time, indicating 5.0 seconds per complete revolution. Sped up by 4×, this translated to 1.25 seconds per revolution—an authentic 48 RPM climbing cadence ramping to 96 RPM sprint cadence, covering ~50 meters in 11.5 seconds (~10 mph). Consecutive frame PSNR delta analysis (consistently 33–35 dB with 0 duplicate frames across all 1,385 frames) mathematically confirmed that a uniform 4× speedup was the true physical real-world pace. Hardware-Accelerated 60fps Reconstruction & DSP Audio Sync With the physical speed factor verified, Antigravity engineered an optimized rendering pipeline leveraging Apple Silicon hardware acceleration: Dual-Stage Audio Time-Stretching: In slow-motion recordings, audio is stretched alongside video. To accelerate the audio track 4× to match the 11.54-second runtime without introducing severe high-pitch “chipmunk” distortion, we implemented chained dual-stage tempo filtering ( atempo=2.0,atempo=2.0 ) at 192 kbps AAC, preserving original voice timbre, spectator cheering, and ambient trail acoustics. VideoToolbox 60fps Fluidity: Because the source contained 120 unique frames of captured motion per real second, rendering at standard 30 fps would discard 75% of the visual data. We configured FFmpeg with Apple's native hardware encoder ( -c:v h264_videotoolbox -b:v 15M ) at 60 fps . This leveraged the dense high-speed capture to produce a broadcast-smooth 60 fps master ( IMG_9739_regular_pace.mov ) in just ~10 seconds of encoding time. Faststart Container Optimization: Second-pass MP4 box relocation ( -movflags +faststart ) shifted the moov index atom ahead of the mdat payload, ensuring instant streaming and zero-delay scrubbing. Metadata Preservation & macOS Photos Automation To ensure the new video integrated seamlessly into my photo library and timeline without appearing as an untagged duplicate, we automated metadata propagation and Photos management: Lossless EXIF & GPS Injection: Using exiftool , we cloned all QuickTime and EXIF metadata tags from the original file, embedding the exact capture date and time ( November 7, 2026 at 8:58:10 AM EST ), camera hardware signature (Apple iPhone 11), orientation, and GPS coordinates ( 44° 42' 49.68" N, 85° 29' 27.24" W at 296m altitude in Traverse City, MI). AppleScript Photos Ingestion: Scripted Apple Photos to import the reconstructed 60fps movie directly into the library and programmatically bind its library timestamp to the original capture date so it appears in its authentic historical timeline slot. Safe Automated Deletion: Apple Photos' scripting dictionary intentionally restricts direct scripting deletions of library media items. Antigravity resolved this by scripting the Photos UI via System Events: spotlighting the original slo-mo asset ( B3DC3400-9771-4642-81FE-370C16CB3CC8 ), triggering the native Delete 1 Video command, and confirming the modal sheet, safely moving the obsolete 46-second original to the Recently Deleted bin for 30-day recovery protection. AI collaboration credit: I identified the accidental slow-motion recording, established the requirements for real-time smoothness and Photos library integration, and tested the final output. Antigravity AI (Google DeepMind) conducted the forensic CoreMedia container and SQLite adjustment analysis, computed the kinematic cadence verification, engineered the FFmpeg VideoToolbox and audio tempo pipeline, cloned all GPS/EXIF tags, and authored the AppleScript Photos automation.

title: Windows XP Malware Lab: Offline VM Setup, Archive Preparation & Snapshot Recovery
snippet: Windows XP Malware Lab: Offline VM Setup, Archive Preparation & Snapshot Recovery Completed Project Oracle VirtualBox · Windows XP Professional (32-bit) · Python & 7-Zip · Completed November 5, 2026 I wanted a disposable Windows XP environment for future malwa...
content: Windows XP Malware Lab: Offline VM Setup, Archive Preparation & Snapshot Recovery Completed Project Oracle VirtualBox · Windows XP Professional (32-bit) · Python & 7-Zip · Completed November 5, 2026 I wanted a disposable Windows XP environment for future malware experiments, with the sample collections available locally and a snapshot I could return to afterward. Working with OpenAI Codex, I installed XP from my existing ISO, prepared repository archives without executing samples, and removed the VM's network and host-folder connections before handoff. Existing XP installation ISO → Separate VirtualBox VM and virtual disk → Verified read-only transfer ISO → Local sample files and pre-test snapshot Installing XP and recovering from a VirtualBox crash The VM uses 1 GB of RAM, one virtual CPU, a new 10 GB IDE virtual disk, and BIOS firmware. Setup progressed through text-mode installation, disk formatting, graphical setup, and first-start configuration to a working desktop with a local Lab account. I supplied the product key and chose the Automatic Updates preference. VirtualBox's settings interface hung during installation. Codex saved the VM's exact state before I closed its stuck console process, then resumed installation. A later host-side memory-reference error closed the VM process; a fresh boot from the installed disk recovered XP. The boot order was changed to prioritize the virtual hard disk, and the final desktop was checked before preparing the snapshot. Preparing the collections without repeated password prompts Codex downloaded the Da2dalus repository and Endermanch repository as ZIP archives, checked their archive integrity, and recorded SHA-256 hashes. To avoid entering Endermanch's published archive password repeatedly, the preparation pipeline recursively unpacked 190 ZIP archives, including nested ZIPs, and nine 7z archives , producing 8,948 extracted files with no reported extraction failures. Python handled the repository traversal, manifests, hashing, and ISO creation. The existing 7-Zip executable handled archive formats and filter chains that the Python extraction library could not decode. Extracted payloads were handled as data in memory and archive containers, then packaged into a read-only ISO; no sample was executed. Names incompatible with Windows XP or the transfer filesystem were shortened or sanitized, with a mapping preserved in the extraction report. Transfer verification and reusable installation media The combined XP_Malware_Collections.iso contains the extracted Endermanch collection and both original repository ZIPs. All 8,948 extracted files were read back from the ISO and checked against the manifest's sizes and SHA-256 hashes; both original ZIPs were also verified. A reusable copy and checksum file were saved in my software archive's onlydoinvms folder. Inside XP, Repository Archives holds the original downloads, while Enderman Extracted holds the ready-to-use extracted tree and its reports. Both folders are on the desktop. The virtual CD was ejected after copying. Completed outcome and boundaries The VM's virtual network adapter is disabled, shared clipboard and drag-and-drop are disabled, and the pre-existing global writable Downloads share was removed. A snapshot named Ready for malware testing - clean XP and samples preserves the prepared desktop before any sample execution. This project completed the lab setup and sample preparation. It did not execute malware, measure malware behavior, or establish that a VM is an escape-proof containment boundary. Disconnecting the virtual adapter is a VM configuration choice, not evidence of a physically air-gapped host; the snapshot provides a reset point for the guest. AI collaboration credit: I directed the setup, supplied the license-key input, selected the repositories and update preference, and helped dismiss host errors and close the stuck console. OpenAI Codex operated the setup UI, used VirtualBox's command-line tools for recovery and configuration, built and verified the archive-transfer pipeline, copied the files, created the snapshot, and documented the completed project.
