title: Samsung Galaxy Player 4.2 (YP-GI1): Legacy Android Audio Standardization & 3,200-Track Multi-Codec Migration Pipeline
snippet: Samsung Galaxy Player 4.2 (YP-GI1): Legacy Android Audio Standardization & 3,200-Track Multi-Codec Migration Pipeline Completed Project Samsung Galaxy Player 4.2 · Android 2.3 Gingerbread · Python & FFmpeg Multithreading · ID3v2.3 Normalization · Completed Nov...
content: Samsung Galaxy Player 4.2 (YP-GI1): Legacy Android Audio Standardization & 3,200-Track Multi-Codec Migration Pipeline Completed Project Samsung Galaxy Player 4.2 · Android 2.3 Gingerbread · Python & FFmpeg Multithreading · ID3v2.3 Normalization · Completed November 5, 2026 How pair programming with Google DeepMind's Antigravity AI diagnosed legacy Android 2.3 media-scanning failures and engineered an 8-worker parallel Python and FFmpeg pipeline to stream, normalize, and transcode a 34.5 GB audio library for a vintage Samsung Galaxy Player 4.2. Remote SMB Music Stash (B:\ONEFIVE - 34.5 GB) → Multi-Threaded Python Scanner & FFmpeg Pipeline (8 Workers) → Standardized 320k MP3 + ID3v2.3 + Cover Art (Y:\GalaxyPlayer_Music) → FAT32 MicroSD Deployment & TouchWiz MediaScanner The Challenge: Missing Songs on Vintage Android 2.3 Gingerbread I wanted to repurpose my vintage Samsung Galaxy Player 4.2 (YP-GI1) —a dedicated portable media device running Android 2.3.6 (Gingerbread) with Samsung's SoundAlive audio enhancement engine and TouchWiz 3.0 interface—as an offline music player loaded with my full music collection from my remote network share ( B:\00. All Music Playlists Revamped LOCAL ). However, upon loading tracks onto the MicroSD card, the built-in Samsung Music player exhibited frustrating behavior: huge batches of songs were completely missing from the library, forcing clumsy manual playback through hierarchical folder browsing. Curiously, some specific albums—notably my Austin's & Dave's CDs and ripped Windows Media Audio ( .wma ) tracks—indexed and displayed flawlessly in the Music app, while my Study Music playlist only populated about half of its songs and large CD rip folders failed to appear by artist or album altogether. To solve this, I paired with Antigravity , Google DeepMind's agentic AI coding assistant, to forensically audit the entire 34.5 GB (3,318 file) audio stash and engineer an automated migration pipeline. Forensic Audit: What I Learned About Android MediaScanner Limits By probing audio stream metadata, codecs, and container structures with ffprobe and Python across the collection, we systematically uncovered why Gingerbread's background MediaScanner service and Stagefright media framework were failing: The M4A / AAC Container Blindspot: In 00. Study Music XII.VIII , our inventory revealed exactly 461 .mp3 files and 461 .m4a files (922 tracks total). Android 2.3's media scanner failed to parse modern MP4/AAC container brands (such as files generated by modern tools like fre:ac and Suno AI). The scanner indexed the 461 MP3s but silently ignored the 461 M4As, explaining why exactly half the playlist vanished. Furthermore, another 413 tracks in 01. Non Study Music - AI were entirely M4A files that were completely invisible to the stock app. FLAC Vorbis Comment Incompatibility: Across Dads Other CDs , Dads Other CDs2 , and Kutless2 , there were 422 .flac lossless files . While Gingerbread could play individual FLAC audio streams if launched manually from a file manager, its stock TouchWiz MediaScanner implementation frequently failed to ingest Vorbis comment metadata into the SQLite media database ( external.db ), leaving tracks orphaned without artist, album, or track numbers. Unsupported Modern Codecs: Modern Opus audio files ( .opus ) were present in recent game soundtracks; Android did not introduce native Opus decoding support until Android 5.0 Lollipop. Why WMA Worked: The Galaxy Player line included dedicated hardware and software licensing for Microsoft Windows Media Audio (WMA) resulting from Samsung's historical mobile partnerships, confirming why older ripped WMA files had successfully played in the past. The Golden Benchmark (Austin's CDs): Inspection of Austins, Daves, Forrest Gump OST CDs revealed that 100% of its tracks were standard Constant Bitrate (CBR) 320 kbps MP3s sampled at 44.1 kHz stereo with clean ID3v2.3 tags and embedded JPEG album art. This exact format represented the universal sweet spot for Gingerbread's parser. FAT32 & Memory Buffer Walls: In VGM - Full , a single monolithic 3.65 GB soundtrack file ( Super Smash Bros Ultimate OST.mp3 ) pushed against the hard 4 GB FAT32 file size limit and risked crashing Gingerbread's memory-constrained MediaScanner process on a device equipped with only 512 MB of total system RAM. Archive Redundancy & macOS Clutter: Unzipping artifacts had created duplicate nested directories (e.g. Study Music\Study Music\... ) alongside hidden __MACOSX resource forks and .DS_Store files that cluttered filesystem traversal. Engineering the 8-Worker Parallel Python & FFmpeg Staging Pipeline Because my music library resided on a remote network share over Tailscale ( \\100.87.81.52\ONEFIVE ) and the Galaxy Player sat near my workstation while I was away, we engineered a dedicated local staging and transcoding engine ( sync_to_galaxy.py ) running on local fixed storage ( Y:\GalaxyPlayer_Music ): Multithreaded ThreadPoolExecutor: Deployed 8 concurrent worker threads leveraging the workstation's 16 CPU cores, achieving streaming network throughput and transcode speeds exceeding 60x real-time (~2.5 files/second). Lossless Direct Copy for Native MP3s: Directly mirrored all 1,427 pre-existing standard MP3 tracks without re-encoding, preserving exact acoustic fidelity and avoiding unnecessary generation loss. Targeted 320k MP3 Transcoding: Dynamically routed all 1,889 non-MP3 files ( .m4a , .flac , .wma , .opus ) through ffmpeg with -c:a libmp3lame -b:a 320k -ar 44100 -id3v2_version 3 -write_id3v1 1 . This converted every track into Austin's gold-standard format while writing dual ID3v2.3 and legacy ID3v1 tags for 100% Gingerbread backwards compatibility. Cover Art Preservation & Fallbacks: Extracted and passed through existing JPEG cover art streams ( -c:v copy ) directly into ID3v2 APIC frames, with an automatic fallback ( -vn ) to strip corrupt or incompatible image formats if muxing encountered errors. Crash-Resilient Atomic Writes: Wrote all transcoded and copied streams to temporary files ( *.tmp.mp3 ) with explicit -f mp3 container declarations before executing atomic file replacements ( os.replace ). This guaranteed zero half-written or corrupt files if network transfers fluctuated. Directory Flattening & Conflict Prioritization: Programmatically stripped redundant double-folder nesting and purged all Mac metadata forks. Resolved duplicate filename collisions using deterministic audio quality hierarchy rules ( FLAC > M4A > MP3 > WMA ). Completed Outcome & MicroSD Deployment The automated pipeline processed all 3,318 library items in 27.4 minutes with zero data corruption (the only 2 skipped files were 0-byte incomplete artifacts from an old LimeWire download folder). The resulting collection comprises 3,190 pristine MP3 tracks (34.52 GB) and 126 album art files, completely standardized in a clean single-level hierarchy ready to be copied directly onto the FAT32 MicroSD card for the Samsung Galaxy Player 4.2. AI collaboration credit: Problem diagnosis, codec analysis, and pipeline architecture co-developed with Antigravity , Google DeepMind's agentic AI coding assistant. Antigravity engineered the multi-threaded Python/FFmpeg transcoding engine, atomic temp-file handling, and metadata normalization scripts, while Andrew directed testing against the physical hardware specifications and verified format requirements. That exposed the old compound on the CPU die and made the blockage in the fin stack visible. What I learned with Copilot Inspect the whole cooling path: thermal material transfers heat to the heatsink, but the fins also need clear airflow. The dust buildup was a separate issue from the old compound. Distinguish the die from the package: the small CPU contact surface is different from the larger surrounding package. That distinction helped me understand where the replacement material belonged. Check power connections during reassembly: on this HP, I found that the battery needed to be plugged in for it to boot. This is my observation on this machine; I have not established whether it is a model-wide requirement. Completed outcome The thermal-interface replacement is finished, the laptop boots, and temperatures are looking good in my follow-up use. I have not recorded numerical before-and-after temperatures or a controlled benchmark, so the result is a successful practical repair rather than a measured temperature-reduction claim. content: 2011 MacBook Pro Battery Removal: Stripped Screws, Power Isolation & Learning from Photos In Progress 2011 MacBook Pro · Battery removal · Plastic spudger · Updated November 5, 2026 I started removing the battery from my always-plugged-in 2011 MacBook Pro, hoping to make it lighter. A stripped battery mounting screw, uncertainty about what still held the battery, and another damaged screw near the logic board turned this into a lesson in careful disassembly and verifying assumptions. The obstacle and the change in priority After reporting that the first screw was out, I examined the battery connector and clearance around the logic board. During the attempt, I reported a brief possible spark when a screw or metal screwdriver contacted exposed contacts near the still-connected battery. I stopped to reassess rather than continue rushing the disassembly. I reported no burnt smell; that observation did not establish that the circuitry was undamaged. What I learned with Copilot A photo interpretation can be wrong: Copilot initially thought the battery was disconnected. My next close-up and clarification showed that it was still connected, changing the assessment. Mechanical removal and electrical disconnection are separate: freeing a mounting screw or moving the battery does not prove that the connector is unplugged. The plastic spudger worked: switching to the nonmetal tool let me disconnect the battery, and the final photo shows the empty board socket and exposed pins. Keep uncertain explanations provisional: the chat speculated about interference under the logic board, but it did not verify that logic-board removal was necessary. Current status and remaining work Battery disconnection is the latest confirmed milestone. The overall project remains in progress: final resolution of the remaining fastener and removal path, complete reassembly, and a functional boot test have not been documented. The photos also do not prove whether the reported short caused any damage. snippet: Private Tailscale Reference Reader & Screen Wake Lock Persistence: Continuous Community Study Web App Completed Project Tailscale Mesh HTTPS · Screen Wake Lock API · Alpine Linux OpenRC Supervision · SQLite Caching · Completed November 2, 2026 How pair program...
content: Private Tailscale Reference Reader & Screen Wake Lock Persistence: Continuous Community Study Web App Completed Project Tailscale Mesh HTTPS · Screen Wake Lock API · Alpine Linux OpenRC Supervision · SQLite Caching · Completed November 2, 2026 How pair programming with Google DeepMind's Antigravity AI engineered a persistent, private reference reading web app on an Alpine Linux homelab server—integrating the HTML5 Screen Wake Lock API, multi-version reference indexing, and encrypted Tailscale HTTPS to eliminate display sleep timeouts during community study discussions. Personal Device (iOS / Android / macOS) → Encrypted Tailnet (Tailscale Serve HTTPS :8444) → Alpine NUC (OpenRC Daemon :8092) → SQLite Cache & Upstream API The Real-World Dilemma: Display Sleep Timeouts During Group Discussion During weekly life group discussions and shared community reading sessions, following along with long-form texts, comparative translations, and reference passages on mobile phones or tablets presents a constant frustration: default device power management. After 30 to 60 seconds of conversational pause or active dialogue, phone screens automatically dim and lock. Having to repeatedly reach out, tap the screen, enter passcodes, or authenticate with biometrics to re-read a passage disrupts the natural rhythm of collaborative study. While native operating system settings allow temporarily disabling screen timeouts globally, doing so is clumsy, drains battery life throughout the remainder of the day, and poses security concerns when forgotten. I wanted a purposeful, lightweight reading web app that automatically keeps the display awake while viewing a reference text, gracefully yields back to standard device sleep policies when closed, and remains securely accessible across all my devices without managing third-party accounts or public exposure. Overcoming Power Management: The Screen Wake Lock API & Visibility State Machine Working with Antigravity AI, we leveraged the modern W3C navigator.wakeLock API to acquire a display lock directly through the browser. However, implementing real-world screen retention on mobile devices involves critical nuances: Visibility State Lifecycle Management: When a user switches to another app, checks a message, or briefly locks their phone, mobile Safari (iOS) and Chromium (Android) automatically and silently release the active wake lock to preserve battery. We implemented an automatic lifecycle watcher via document.addEventListener('visibilitychange', ...) . When the reader tab returns to visible , the application automatically inspects user preferences and immediately re-acquires the screen wake lock without requiring manual intervention. Explicit Visual Telemetry: In a group setting, certainty matters. We engineered a prominent, tactile top-docked control with active visual feedback (a pulsing emerald telemetry indicator indicating “Screen Awake: ON — Display will stay on” versus a muted slate indicator for “Screen Awake: OFF — Tap to keep display on” ). Full Cross-Session Persistence: Display wake-lock toggles, selected translations (WEB, KJV, ASV, BBE, OEB), active chapter position, font scale (small through extra-large), typography style (Serif vs. Sans), and reading palette (Dark, Warm Sepia, and Clean Light) are synchronized to localStorage , instantly resuming the exact reading environment across browser restarts. Resolving the Secure Context Requirement with Private Tailscale HTTPS A crucial technical constraint of the Screen Wake Lock API is security sandboxing: modern browsers strictly refuse to expose navigator.wakeLock in non-secure contexts. Accessing a local service over plain HTTP (e.g., http://100.87.81.52:8092 ) results in the browser marking window.isSecureContext === false , disabling the API entirely. To satisfy the secure context requirement while maintaining absolute privacy, we integrated Tailscale Serve on the stationary Alpine Linux NUC ( nucWOL2-0--HDD ): Tailnet-Only HTTPS: Tailscale Serve was provisioned to listen on dedicated port 8444 ( https://nucwol2-0--hdd.taile72a68.ts.net:8444/ ) and reverse-proxy internal traffic to the local daemon at 127.0.0.1:8092 . Trusted Automated TLS: Tailscale automatically terminates Let's Encrypt TLS certificates matching the node's MagicDNS domain. This establishes a fully trusted HTTPS secure context, enabling complete native Wake Lock API functionality on iPhone and Android browsers. Zero Funnel Exposure: Tailscale Funnel was strictly kept disabled for port 8444. Unlike the public portfolio gateway, this service is only reachable from authenticated nodes on my private tailnet. There are no public login forms or exposed surface areas to the wider internet. Reliable Homelab Daemon Architecture & SQLite Offline Caching To ensure zero maintenance overhead, the backend was engineered as a self-contained, zero-dependency Python service managed by Alpine Linux's native OpenRC init system: OpenRC Supervise Daemon: Configured a dedicated service script ( /etc/init.d/bible-reader ) supervised by supervise-daemon with automated respawn limits, standard logging, and registered in the default runlevel ( rc-update add bible-reader default ) to guarantee uninterrupted availability across system reboots. Sub-Millisecond SQLite Caching: The daemon integrates a persistent SQLite database ( bible_cache.db ) that indexes all retrieved chapters and verse queries. Once a passage is requested, subsequent lookups are resolved from local storage in less than 2 milliseconds with an X-Cache: HIT header, ensuring rapid navigation even when church or community basement Wi-Fi connectivity is degraded. Fast Navigation Ergonomics: Features single-thumb touch navigation, modal drawer book selection across both the Old and New Testaments, chapter number grids, and interactive verse tapping that copies formatted citations directly to the system clipboard with an animated toast notification. AI collaboration credit: Developed in pair programming with Google DeepMind's Antigravity AI to architect the Screen Wake Lock state machine, implement visibility change re-acquisition listeners, configure OpenRC init supervision on Alpine Linux, and provision private Tailscale HTTPS termination. title: Making a Desktop Project Plan a Shared Team Workspace
snippet: Making a Desktop Project Plan a Shared Team Workspace Completed Project CIS 450 · Project Plan 365 · Microsoft Teams · Cross-platform browser testing · Completed November 1, 2026 For a CIS 450 group project, I wanted everyone to help build the project schedule...
content: Making a Desktop Project Plan a Shared Team Workspace Completed Project CIS 450 · Project Plan 365 · Microsoft Teams · Cross-platform browser testing · Completed November 1, 2026 For a CIS 450 group project, I wanted everyone to help build the project schedule instead of leaving one person to enter the entire plan. I already had an activated copy of Project Plan 365 on Windows. The question was whether I could make that existing application available to classmates in a simple, practical way. Start with the actual license and requirements Working with OpenAI’s ChatGPT/Codex, I inspected the application’s About screen and confirmed a perpetual, per-device Standard Editor license for PC/Server. A visible Sign In button did not mean the installed editor was unactivated. We checked the vendor’s documentation and established that native real-time collaboration requires its Business offering, Editor access for collaborators, and a project stored in Drive 365. Saving and emailing an MPP file would let people exchange copies, but would not create one live shared editing session. Compare alternatives before adding infrastructure I considered hosting one master application instance inside a virtual machine, with classmates joining a shared remote desktop. We researched Apache Guacamole as a browser gateway and discussed a dedicated VM as a way to separate the class workspace from my personal computer. I also had a working macOS VM, but its possible latency made it a less attractive starting point for a live group session. These were options we evaluated; we did not deploy a Guacamole server or move the Windows activation into the Mac VM. I chose to test meeting software I already had available. Zoom offered screen sharing and remote control; Teams was familiar from my internship. The goal became one Windows application, one master project file, and classmates taking turns entering and reviewing tasks while everyone watched. Test the real cross-platform workflow I hosted a Teams meeting in the Windows desktop app, shared the Project Plan 365 window, and joined from a browser on my Mac. I successfully requested and received control, saw the participant cursor, and interacted with the shared application. I then tested joining without signing into an account and confirmed that browser-based control also worked in that session. Approve requests from the original meeting window: the floating sharing toolbar was difficult to find, but I could accept the control request in the main Teams meeting window. Keep the shared application open and not minimized: this was important in my test. Switching windows could pause application sharing, and minimizing the shared window disrupted the intended workflow. Coordinate editing: everyone shares the same application view and keyboard focus. This supports taking turns on one plan; it does not add independent, simultaneous task editing or merge separate users’ changes. Verify the account environment: anonymous browser control worked in my test, but another organization’s meeting policies or client configuration may behave differently. Fit the solution into the existing group routine We created a recurring Teams meeting matching the group’s Tuesday/Thursday, 6–7 p.m. schedule through December 8. Codex added its join link to the existing CIS 450 GC Google Calendar invitation for November 3 and following occurrences, preserving the original Zoom details. After I approved sending the update, the invitation was saved and update emails were sent to the existing guests. The group could use the invitation it already had rather than receive a separate Teams invitation. Outcome and lesson The result was a working, manually tested way to share control of an existing desktop planning application across Windows and a Mac browser. It gave us a practical way to divide responsibility for entering tasks and dependencies without first deploying another remote-access platform. Shared control still requires trust: showing one app window should not be treated as a sandbox that guarantees isolation from the host computer. This experiment reflects how I approach a constraint: identify what the current software actually supports, investigate alternatives, test the simplest promising workflow, and document its limits. The access test and calendar setup are complete; long-session performance with the full class group remains to be evaluated. AI collaboration credit: OpenAI’s ChatGPT/Codex helped inspect the installed license, research vendor documentation and alternatives, troubleshoot the Teams controls, configure the recurring link and calendar update, and write this project account. I defined the classroom need, chose the workflow, performed the Mac browser and anonymous-access tests, discovered the main-window approval path, and approved notifying the group. References: Project Plan 365 collaboration requirements · Teams control-sharing policies · Guacamole connection sharing Project Plan 365 Microsoft Teams Windows macOS browser Google Calendar Workflow evaluation

title: macOS Blackboard Single Sign-On Automation: UI Scripting, Apple Events Security & Safari Credential Isolation
snippet: macOS Blackboard Single Sign-On Automation: UI Scripting, Apple Events Security & Safari Credential Isolation In-Progress Project macOS zsh · AppleScript / System Events · Safari Touch ID · SSO Authentication · In-Progress Updated September 12, 2026 At Grand V...
content: macOS Blackboard Single Sign-On Automation: UI Scripting, Apple Events Security & Safari Credential Isolation In-Progress Project macOS zsh · AppleScript / System Events · Safari Touch ID · SSO Authentication · In-Progress Updated September 12, 2026 At Grand Valley State University, accessing coursework on Blackboard requires repeatedly navigating through multi-step Single Sign-On (SSO) login screens and two-factor authentication (2FA/MFA) prompts. To streamline my daily academic workflow on macOS without compromising security, I set out to engineer a desktop automation shortcut that launches Safari and minimizes repetitive credential entry. Initial Desktop Launcher & Keystroke Simulation Vulnerability I began by authoring a double-clickable macOS desktop shortcut ( GVSU Blackboard Login.command ) written in Zsh to open https://my.gvsu.edu/ inside Apple Safari via /usr/bin/open -b com.apple.Safari . To automate the login form, I initially experimented with storing credentials within an AppleScript wrapper and injecting keystrokes into form inputs using macOS System Events. The Critical Security Realization: During testing, an unexpected window focus shift occurred—a background notification momentarily stole active window focus, causing scripted keystrokes containing credentials to be typed directly into an open Google search field rather than the targeted authentication field. Recognizing this fundamental security flaw, I immediately halted the approach, purged all stored plaintext credentials from the script, and updated account passwords across the board. This experience underscored a core rule of systems engineering: never rely on blind keystroke injection for authentication . Accessibility & Coordinate Automation Roadblocks I then investigated targeting Safari's DOM elements directly through macOS accessibility labels via System Events (querying UI elements such as “Next” , “Verify with something else” , and “Receive a code via SMS” ). However, because modern web browsers isolate web content within sandboxed WebContent processes, standard macOS accessibility trees cannot reliably bind to dynamic web controls across varying page states. Next, I tested fixed-coordinate mouse clicks paired with programmatic delays (including a 10-second window for Touch ID verification). This quickly proved brittle: display scaling differences, dynamic browser window positioning, and variable network latency caused coordinate-based clicks to miss buttons or inadvertently trigger unwanted autofill popovers. Re-Architecting Around Native Touch ID & Credential Isolation Rather than compromising security to force full automation, I pivoted the architecture to a safe, defense-in-depth model: Zero Credential Storage: The launcher shortcut stores zero passwords and performs zero keystroke injection. Leveraging Secure Enclave & Touch ID: The shortcut safely opens the institutional portal in Safari, allowing macOS Keychain and Safari Password AutoFill to manage credentials backed by biometric Touch ID authentication. Manual Confirmation for MFA: Preserves a strict manual confirmation step for multi-factor SMS/app approvals, ensuring automated processes cannot trigger unauthorized 2FA challenges. Current Status & Next Engineering Steps The project is currently operational as a hardened, safe launch shortcut. To safely advance automation without compromising isolation, I am evaluating two paths: Safari-Native JavaScript Apple Events: Utilizing do JavaScript via AppleScript to query dynamic DOM elements by text and class name. This requires enabling Safari's “Allow JavaScript from Apple Events” developer permission, which introduces trust boundaries that must be evaluated thoroughly. Dedicated Browser Extension Architecture: Evaluating a scoped WebExtension that operates strictly within the context of the authentication domain, eliminating the fragility of external OS-level window hooks. AI collaboration credit: Developed in pair programming with AI assistance to evaluate macOS System Events accessibility architectures, document security threat boundaries, and formulate the risk-averse refactoring from keystroke injection to biometric isolation. All testing, vulnerability identification, and architectural security decisions were directed and validated by Andrew Van Ek. macOS Zsh AppleScript Safari Automation System Events Single Sign-On (SSO) MFA Security Touch ID In-Progress

title: Persistent Homelab LLM Inference & Private Tailscale Mesh Streaming: Deploying GLM-4-9B-Chat with Antigravity AI
snippet: Persistent Homelab LLM Inference & Private Tailscale Mesh Streaming: Deploying GLM-4-9B-Chat with Antigravity AI Completed Project LM Studio Headless Daemon · GLM-4-9B-Chat GGUF · Encrypted Tailnet · Custom Streaming Web UI · Systemd Supervision · Completed Oc...
content: Persistent Homelab LLM Inference & Private Tailscale Mesh Streaming: Deploying GLM-4-9B-Chat with Antigravity AI Completed Project LM Studio Headless Daemon · GLM-4-9B-Chat GGUF · Encrypted Tailnet · Custom Streaming Web UI · Systemd Supervision · Completed October 29, 2026 How pair programming with Google DeepMind's Antigravity AI transformed an 8-vCPU homelab Linux VM into an always-on, private AI reasoning node—serving GLM-4-9B over Tailscale with a dedicated zero-dependency streaming web app, RAM pre-loading, and resilient multi-user service supervision. Any Tailscale Device (iOS / macOS / Windows / Linux) → Encrypted Tailnet (100.82.213.77) → Zero-Dependency Node.js Web UI & Proxy (Port 3000) → LM Studio llmster Daemon & OpenAI API (Port 12340) → GLM-4-9B-Chat (Q4_K_M GGUF in RAM) The Vision: Dedicated Private AI Reasoning on the Tailnet While cloud-hosted models and subscription chatbots are powerful, they present significant trade-offs for personal homelab workflows: recurring monthly subscription overhead, third-party privacy exposure, rate limits, and an inability to easily query models from headless internal scripts or mobile devices without exposing endpoints to the public WAN. Having an 8-vCPU virtual machine with 31 GiB of RAM ( fah-cpu-8 ) connected to my private Tailscale mesh network, I set out to establish an always-on, private local large language model (LLM) server. I selected GLM-4-9B-Chat (quantized to 4-bit Q4_K_M GGUF, consuming 6.25 GB of memory). GLM-4 delivers an outstanding balance for local compute: advanced multi-turn instruction following, deep analytical reasoning, coding proficiency, and native support for up to 8,192 context tokens on CPU inference without requiring an expensive enterprise GPU cluster. The objective was straightforward: boot persistence, zero manual terminal startup, an OpenAI-compatible REST API for developer tooling, and a dedicated, lightweight mobile-friendly web chat interface accessible anywhere on my Tailscale network. Headless Runtime & Persistent Systemd Supervision Rather than relying on manual GUI applications that require an active X11 desktop session, I paired with Antigravity , Google DeepMind's agentic AI coding assistant, to engineer an autonomous background service stack: Headless LM Studio Core ( llmster ): Deployed the native Linux x86_64 headless daemon (v0.0.25-1) and CLI toolchain ( lms ), configuring the runtime engine to optimize CPU thread pools across all 8 virtual cores with AVX2/AVX512 acceleration. Private Tailnet Binding & CORS: Configured the server to bind exclusively to the host's private network stack ( 0.0.0.0:12340 ) with CORS enabled, exposing a standard OpenAI-compatible completions endpoint ( /v1/chat/completions ) and models catalog ( /v1/models ) strictly accessible by authenticated tailnet peers ( 100.82.213.77 ). Systemd Service Architecture: Authored a system-level supervisor unit ( /etc/systemd/system/lmstudio.service ) backed by a startup supervisor script ( /home/fold/.local/bin/lmstudio-service.sh ). The service starts after network and Tailscale daemons, initializes the daemon, starts the API listener, and executes an automated pre-load of glm-4-9b-chat into RAM on boot. By pre-allocating the 6.25 GB model weights into memory during VM startup, client requests receive instant token generation without encountering cold-start load delays. Desktop Access: Generated a customized freedesktop launcher ( LM Studio.desktop ) on the user desktop for direct GUI discovery whenever interactive local sessions are utilized. Overcoming Deployment Roadblocks: Storage Crunches, Symlink Drift & Temp Paths Engineering a clean, headless multi-component service on a compact 30 GB virtual root partition surfaced several real-world operational challenges that we systematically diagnosed and resolved: The 99% Capacity Wall & Orphaned Part Recovery: Following an abrupt terminal disconnection during initial model acquisition, the root filesystem hit a critical threshold: 28 GB used with only 315 MB free (99% capacity) . A forensic inspection revealed that an interrupted 4.1 GB download artifact ( downloading_glm-4-9b-chat-Q4_K_M.gguf.part ) remained trapped on disk alongside the fully finalized 6.25 GB model file. Safely purging the partial residue reclaimed 4.1 GB instantly, restoring system disk headroom to a safe 4.4 GB. Chat-Template Temp Directory Provisioning: Headless model loading initially failed with a Node.js filesystem exception ( Error: ENOENT: no such file or directory, mkdtemp '/home/fold/.lmstudio/.internal/temp/lmstudio-chat-template-...' ). The headless runtime expected a persistent internal temporary working folder that had not been generated by the installer. We updated the service script to proactively ensure ~/.lmstudio/.internal/temp exists with proper ownership before invoking model loads. PATH & Symlink Normalization: Resolved an invocation disconnect where the installer reported successful registration in shell profiles but left broken symlinks in ~/.local/bin/lms . Established deterministic symlinks directly into the active llmster bundle directory ( ~/.lmstudio/llmster/0.0.25-1/.bundle/lms ), enabling seamless command execution across systemd scripts and interactive SSH sessions alike. Engineering the Zero-Dependency Streaming Web Interface While the native LM Studio AppImage provides a desktop UI, mobile devices such as iPhones and remote tablets on Tailscale cannot run native Linux desktop binaries. To deliver a seamless conversational experience without the bloat of multi-gigabyte containerized frontends or third-party web frameworks, we engineered a dedicated, custom web application ( /home/fold/.local/share/lmstudio-webui/server.mjs ): Pure Node.js Architecture: Built using only native Node.js standard modules ( http , fs , path , URL )—requiring zero external npm dependencies or package bloat. Real-Time Server-Sent Events (SSE) Streaming: The web proxy transparently forwards chat completion requests to LM Studio's backend with stream: true and parses incoming SSE data chunks ( data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"content":"..."}}]} ), streaming text live to the browser DOM token-by-token. Mobile Soft-Keyboard & Form Navigation Defense: During initial testing on mobile browsers, pressing the virtual “Send” or “Go” key caused the browser to execute a standard HTML GET form submission to /? , triggering an abrupt “Not found” error. We hardened both ends of the pipeline: converted the client form to event-driven JavaScript submission with navigation prevention ( action="javascript:void(0);" , onsubmit="return false;" ), and upgraded the Node server router with dynamic URL pathname parsing and a resilient fallback handler that always serves the chat UI for any incoming GET request. Responsive Dark-Mode Cockpit: Implemented a clean, modern interface featuring automatic textarea expansion, clear-history action, live model selector filtering out embedding models, and an active pulse indicator confirming backend server connectivity. Verification & Telemetry We conducted end-to-end verification across the entire network topology. Both endpoints are active and healthy: Dedicated Web Chat: http://100.82.213.77:3000 — Verified responsive token streaming on iPhone and workstation browsers across Tailscale with zero packet drops. Direct OpenAI REST API: http://100.82.213.77:12340/v1 — Verified multi-turn completions with curl and Python OpenAI SDK scripts: curl http://100.82.213.77:12340/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "glm-4-9b-chat", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain homelab mesh routing in 2 sentences."}] }' Inference Telemetry: Tested prompt evaluation and generation throughput on the 8-vCPU Intel Xeon compute node: prompt evaluation completed at 418 ms/token (~2.4 tok/s) and generation sustained ~2.2–2.4 tokens/second across an 8,192 token context window, providing reliable, private, and capable AI reasoning directly within my homelab. Stack GLM-4-9B-Chat (Q4_K_M GGUF) LM Studio Headless (llmster 0.0.25-1) Tailscale Mesh VPN Debian 12 Linux (8 vCPUs / 31 GiB RAM) Node.js (Native HTTP & SSE Proxy) Systemd Service Supervision llama.cpp AVX2/AVX512 CPU Backend HTML5 / CSS3 Responsive UI AI collaboration credit: Designed, deployed, debugged, and documented in continuous pair-programming collaboration with Antigravity , Google DeepMind's agentic AI coding assistant. Operating autonomously through direct terminal and system execution harnesses, Antigravity handled disk forensics, systemd service writing, shell scripting, API verification, and full-stack web development across the entire project lifecycle.

title: Autonomous Drive C Forensics & Precision Reclamation: Reclaiming 65+ GB on Windows with Antigravity AI
snippet: Autonomous Drive C Forensics & Precision Reclamation: Reclaiming 65+ GB on Windows with Antigravity AI In Progress Parallel File Tree Forensics · Reparse Point Auditing · PyTorch Checkpoint Pruning · Antigravity AI Pair Programming · Active October 28, 2026 Ho...
content: Autonomous Drive C Forensics & Precision Reclamation: Reclaiming 65+ GB on Windows with Antigravity AI In Progress Parallel File Tree Forensics · Reparse Point Auditing · PyTorch Checkpoint Pruning · Antigravity AI Pair Programming · Active October 28, 2026 How systematic parallel filesystem inspection with Google DeepMind's Antigravity AI diagnosed a critical 93.2% capacity bottleneck on my primary Windows SSD, recovered over 65 GB in safe multi-stage sweeps, and established a zero-loss roadmap to reclaim 40+ GB more. The Capacity Wall: 93.2% Full on Primary Drive C As a developer running local machine learning fine-tuning, multiple virtualization platforms, and containerized dev environments on a primary workstation, disk storage is constantly under high pressure. On October 28, 2026, my primary 500 GB NVMe solid-state drive ( C:\ ) hit a critical threshold: Total Capacity: 475.93 GB Used Space: 443.74 GB ( 93.2% capacity ) Free Space Remaining: Only 32.19 GB With an active PyTorch fine-tuning workflow producing multi-epoch checkpoints, multiple VM disk images, and heavy developer caching, running below 35 GB of headroom created immediate risks of filesystem thrashing, aborted training epochs, and broken Windows virtual memory paging. I needed a systematic, zero-data-loss storage audit to pinpoint exactly what was eating the drive and safely reclaim tens of gigabytes without disrupting running environments. Algorithmic Filesystem Forensics: Eliminating Recursion & Junction Traps Standard Windows tools like File Explorer and naive PowerShell recursive commands ( Get-ChildItem -Recurse ) quickly proved unusable for a drive this large: they either froze indefinitely, spawned millions of .NET object allocations that devoured system RAM, or got trapped in infinite recursion loops caused by Windows filesystem junctions (such as the legacy Application Data loop pointing back into AppData\Local ). To solve this, I paired up with Antigravity , Google DeepMind's agentic AI coding assistant. Operating directly in my workstation terminal through autonomous PowerShell and Python execution harnesses, Antigravity built a high-speed multi-threaded filesystem crawler that bypassed standard pitfalls: Low-Level Reparse Point Detection: Inspected the Win32 file attribute bitmask ( st_file_attributes & 0x400 ) to identify and safely bypass directory junctions and cloud-reparse placeholders (preventing infinite loops and unwanted OneDrive file hydration). Concurrent Multi-Worker Directory Walks: Leveraged Python's ThreadPoolExecutor with 8 parallel worker threads using os.scandir directly against Windows NT filesystem APIs, scanning hundreds of thousands of files across deep subtrees in seconds. The forensic scan revealed the primary storage offenders across Drive C: C:\Users\Owner : 232.93 GB (over 52.5% of the entire drive), dominated by AppData (73.6 GB), Downloads (56.4 GB), AI_Apps (19.3 GB), and VirtualBox VMs (21.2 GB). C:\ProgramData : 20.23 GB , heavily consumed by a 13.88 GB BlueStacks Android emulator container. C:\Windows : 55.63 GB , including 20.4 GB in WinSxS and a massive 15.0 GB in System32\DriverStore (accumulated superseded driver packages). Root System Files: 18.92 GB locked by hiberfil.sys (12.67 GB) and pagefile.sys (6.25 GB). Phase 1: What We Have Cleaned Up (+65.10 GB Reclaimed) Working collaboratively through interactive planning, we executed an incremental, safe series of surgical purges: Slax Linux Session Backups & Build Artifacts (7.54 GB Physical Reclaim): Permanently removed slax_session1_backup (which held multiple multi-gigabyte sparse changes.dat.* persistence files) and Slax-build (custom ISO outputs like slax-debian-xfce-custom.iso and Slackware module archives). FreeBSD VirtualBox VM Decommissioning (3.18 GB): Cleanly unregistered the powered-off VM using Oracle's CLI tool: & "C:\Program Files\Oracle\VirtualBox\VBoxManage.exe" unregistervm "FreeBSD 64 bits" --delete This safely purged the virtual disk ( FreeBSD 64 bits.vdi ) and configuration without leaving orphaned entries in the VirtualBox machine registry. Orphaned Kali VM Snapshot Removal (5.31 GB): The audit detected an orphaned 4.11 GB saved state snapshot ( 2026-09-13...sav ) in VirtualBox VMs\Kali 64 BITS\Snapshots belonging to a VM that was no longer registered in VirtualBox, safely eliminating it while leaving active VMs (such as 458project ) completely untouched. Deep Dive on PyTorch LoRA Resumption & Checkpoint Pruning (35.0 GB): My Downloads/ACE_STEP_Dataset_Clean_30s directory held over 51 GB of training outputs across multiple runs. I wanted to verify whether deleting early epoch checkpoints would break my ability to resume training from later checkpoints. Together with Antigravity, we inspected my training scripts ( resume_training_to_epoch100.py and train.py ) and verified that every checkpoint directory is 100% self-contained : adapter_model.safetensors (84 MB) stores the complete cumulative LoRA weights up to that epoch. training_state.pt (168.3 MB) contains the complete AdamW optimizer momentum buffers, learning rate scheduler state, and global step count. When resuming training via --resume-from <checkpoint_dir> , PyTorch loads strictly from that target folder and never references earlier epochs. With this confirmed, we performed an extensive pruning sweep: Deleted obsolete early run lora_output_validated_epoch45 ( 7.48 GB ). Deleted obsolete run lora_output_validated_epoch100 ( 9.94 GB ). Deleted 8 miscellaneous early test runs (epochs 1, 4, 6, 7, 12, 25, 60, and continuation tests, reclaiming 7.97 GB ). Pruned 39 intermediate checkpoints from lora_output_validated_epoch180 while preserving epoch_180_loss_0.8729 and the exported final adapter for future audio sound benchmarking (reclaiming 9.61 GB ). BlueStacks Android Container Purge (13.88 GB): Permanently removed C:\ProgramData\BlueStacks_nxt , wiping unused Android VHD virtual disks and cache. OneDrive Local Cache Dehydration: Executed attrib +U -P /s /d across duplicate GGUF models ( Z3. LM Studio Models ) and portable app runtimes in OneDrive - Grand Valley State University (1) to instruct OneDrive's Cloud Files engine to evict local disk sectors while preserving cloud availability. Phase 1 Result: Free disk space on Drive C expanded from 32.19 GB to 97.29 GB —a net recovery of 65.10 GB of high-speed NVMe storage , bringing drive capacity down from 93.2% to 79.5% . Phase 2: In-Progress Roadmap (Identified Targets for 40+ GB More) Because this project is active and ongoing, we cataloged and staged the next batch of high-yield reclamation targets to execute in subsequent pair-programming sessions: Prune Intermediate Checkpoints in Epoch 200 (~4.75 GB): Apply the same surgical pruning to lora_output_validated_epoch200 —preserving our all-time lowest loss checkpoint ( epoch_200_loss_0.8885 , step 4,600) and the final adapter while clearing intermediate epochs 181–199. Orphaned Windows 11 VM Snapshot (5.51 GB): Remove VirtualBox VMs\Windows 11\Snapshots\2026-09-13...sav (an orphaned saved-state file from an unregistered VM with no base disk). Python Package Wheels & Build Caches (11.1 GB): Run uv cache clean ( 8.0 GB ) and pip cache purge ( 3.1 GB ) in AppData\Local to wipe downloaded package archives without affecting any installed virtual environment. User Temp Scratches (4.18 GB): Purge scratch installers and crash logs in AppData\Local\Temp . Academic Lab Forensics Image (7.0 GB): Archive Documents\cis430\lab05\evidence\InCh05.img (6.0 GB raw forensic dump) to external homelab cold storage. Disable Windows Fast Startup / Hibernation (12.67 GB): Execute powercfg /h off from an elevated administrator command prompt to permanently remove C:\hiberfil.sys . WSL2 Debian Virtual Disk Compaction (up to 15 GB): Run diskpart compaction against AppData\Local\wsl\...\ext4.vhdx (currently 24.1 GB on host while only 19 GB is used internally). Session Telemetry & Resuming with Antigravity AI To ensure continuity and reproducibility across sessions, the entire investigation trajectory, environment state, and diagnostic tooling are maintained in Google DeepMind's Antigravity assistant system. Antigravity CLI Conversation ID: 362b53f1-3a98-4019-bde4-e886b81f209a How to Resume This Project Session: From any terminal on the workstation running Antigravity CLI, run: agy --resume 362b53f1-3a98-4019-bde4-e886b81f209a Or open the Antigravity session manager and select this conversation to continue directly from the current filesystem state.
