snippet: Cross-Volume Archive Deduplication & Dual-Drive Mirroring: Deconstructing Google Takeout with Antigravity AI Completed Project Tailscale SMB · exFAT vs. NTFS Delta Sync · PowerShell Forensics · Antigravity AI Pair Programming · Completed October 28, 2026 How p...
content: Cross-Volume Archive Deduplication & Dual-Drive Mirroring: Deconstructing Google Takeout with Antigravity AI Completed Project Tailscale SMB · exFAT vs. NTFS Delta Sync · PowerShell Forensics · Antigravity AI Pair Programming · Completed October 28, 2026 How pair programming with Google DeepMind's Antigravity AI turned a 70 GB nested Google Takeout maze and network sync bottleneck into an automated, zero-data-loss storage audit and 5-minute smart delta sync. The Storage Sprawl Dilemma: Multi-Part Takeout & Fragmented Roots Over years of backups, data sprawl is inevitable. Across my homelab storage array—specifically drive B:\ ( ONEFIVE , a 500 GB NTFS partition hosted on my stationary Alpine Linux NUC and accessed remotely via Tailscale authenticated SMB) and drive G:\ ( ONETB , a 1 TB high-capacity local exFAT drive)—both root filesystems contained a legacy folder named Z4. Drive Takeout . Google Takeout exports are notoriously unwieldy: multi-part zip archives unpack into nested folder trees four to six levels deep ( Z4. Drive Takeout\avanek2005\takeout-20260510T175627Z-3-001\takeout-...\Takeout\Drive\05. All backups\... ). Compounding the confusion, previous partial extractions had left fragmented remnants scattered across the root directories of both drives—including loose files in 23. driveRootFilez , folders like 05. Backups , and raw timestamped export names like 02. Counseling Stuff-20260517T221837Z-3-001 . Simply wiping Z4. Drive Takeout was out of the question: blindly deleting 25,600+ files (~70 GB) carried massive risks of permanently destroying unique personal documents, irreplaceable family concert footage, or unindexed photo albums. Yet manually verifying and sorting every nested directory by hand would have required days of mind-numbing clicking. Algorithmic File Forensics: Pairing with Antigravity AI To eliminate the guesswork and ensure strict zero data loss, I paired up with Antigravity , Google DeepMind's agentic AI coding assistant. Operating directly in the environment through automated PowerShell inspection harnesses, Antigravity systematically indexed, cataloged, and cross-referenced all 25,616 files in Z4. Drive Takeout against the root directory contents of both drives. The forensic audit categorized the 69.64 GB archive into four distinct actionable buckets: Safe Movie Pruning (“Yoinking” 2.62 GB): In takeout-003 , the audit isolated two large movies ( PLANES_FIRE_AND_RESCUE [828 MB] and The_APPLE_DUMPLING_GANG [1.98 GB]). Cross-referencing against G:\09. Movies\PG+G Movies\ proved they were 100% byte-for-byte identical duplicates, allowing them to be safely deleted immediately. Promoting 58 GB of Google Photos: The audit discovered that Takeout\Google Photos held 25,308 files (~58 GB) with zero representation anywhere on the root of either drive. Deleting the Takeout folder would have wiped out the entire photo library. Instead, we executed an instant filesystem rename, promoting the directory directly to root as 03. Google Photos on both drives (taking 0 extra bytes and 0 seconds). Rescuing Loose Root Documents (304 MB): Nine loose Google Drive documents and videos (including a 292 MB recording 20210119_021608A.mp4 , study audio, and presentations) were extracted and consolidated directly into 23. driveRootFilez . Recovering Irreplaceable Backups & Photo Sets (8.96 GB): Deep inside 05. All backups , the audit surfaced five irreplaceable family concert and anniversary videos (6.5 GB from 2012–2017) that existed nowhere else on any drive, plus 290 phone picture backups. These were safely migrated and merged into 05. Backups without overwriting existing files. Once every byte was accounted for and safely housed, Z4. Drive Takeout was completely empty and permanently deleted from both drives. Overcoming SMB Protocol & exFAT vs. NTFS Timestamp Roadblocks With the archive cleared, the next step was bringing B:\ and G:\ into clean mirror synchronization (excluding designated local folders _TEMP on B: and 09. Movies on G: ). However, standard Windows utilities immediately surfaced low-level filesystem incompatibilities: SMB Error 50 ( The request is not supported ): Standard tools like robocopy and xcopy attempting to preserve POSIX directory attributes over the remote Tailscale SMB mount failed because the underlying Linux Samba share rejects certain Windows directory attribute modifications. We adapted the tooling to handle data streams cleanly without triggering attribute errors. The exFAT Timestamp Resolution Trap: When running standard delta sync ( xcopy /D ), the process stalled on 19. WiiU stuf (a 44.8 GB directory) and began re-copying a 14.36 GB archive over the Wi-Fi link. The cause: G:\ is formatted as exFAT (which rounds timestamps to 2-second increments), while B:\ is NTFS (sub-second precision). Standard timestamp comparison falsely flagged identical multi-gigabyte ISOs as “newer” on NTFS, threatening to drag out the sync for over 3 hours across 150+ GB of already-identical game dumps. Engineering the Smart Delta Sync: Hours to 5 Minutes Rather than letting network transfers waste hours re-streaming identical files, we terminated the brute-force transfer and engineered a targeted PowerShell Smart-Sync engine ( smart_sync.ps1 ). The script used existence checks and strict byte-length comparison rather than fragile cross-filesystem timestamps, completely skipping the 150+ GB of verified Wii, Wii U, and ROM archives. The smart engine executed in roughly 5 minutes, targeting only true discrepancies: Transferred 542 missing songs into 00. All Music Playlists Revamped LOCAL (bringing both drives to an identical 41.86 GB audio corpus). Synchronized developer software packages (MySQL macOS/Windows installers, Android x86 ISOs, and IPA archives) between drives in 08 Software . Mirrored OpenVPN profiles, Minecraft server configurations, and Windows XP legacy wallpapers. Normalized takeout suffix folders on G:\ (e.g., 02. Counseling Stuff and 04. Personal Portfolio Website Stuff ) to match B:\ . A post-sync verification audit confirmed 100% parity across all shared directories on both drives, transforming an intimidating, confusing archive sprawl into an organized, fully redundant storage architecture.

title: One Assistant, Two Brains: Self-Updating AI Assistant on Google Cloud
snippet: One Assistant, Two Brains: Self-Updating AI Assistant on Google Cloud Live & Deployed Cloud Run · Vertex AI Search · Google Drive API · Major Rebuild November 14, 2026 How a “can I just add a bot in Teams?” idea became a self-updating AI assistant on Google Cl...
content: One Assistant, Two Brains: Self-Updating AI Assistant on Google Cloud Live & Deployed Cloud Run · Vertex AI Search · Google Drive API · Major Rebuild November 14, 2026 How a “can I just add a bot in Teams?” idea became a self-updating AI assistant on Google Cloud — conceived on a Tuesday, live by Wednesday night. The idea It started with a simple want: a chatbot I could message like a person. I work at the GVSU IT Service Desk, where I answer the same questions over and over — how to register a game console on the dorm network, where a form lives, what laptop a computing student should buy — and my “system” for that knowledge was a stack of bookmarks and KB articles I could never find fast enough. At the same time I’m a student, and my coursework lived in a OneDrive folder of hundreds of files: lecture notes, transcripts, screenshots, worksheets, study guides. None of it searchable as a whole. So: one assistant with two brains. My service-desk knowledge for work, my class materials for studying — and a switch to choose which brain answers. I designed the switch to sit right by the message input, like ChatGPT’s model picker: Service Desk / Classes / Everything. First direction: Microsoft Teams (and why it died) The original plan was a Teams bot I could add like a contact. Research killed it quickly: personal Teams can’t sideload custom bots as contacts, and Zoom bots aren’t contacts either. I also already had a half-built Teams bot sitting in Google Cloud from an earlier attempt — it answered every message with a 503 error, because its Microsoft credentials were never configured. On October 21 I scrapped Teams and Azure entirely: Google Cloud would be the brain, a simple web page would be the face. The simplest thing that could possibly work. What got built A web chat app (Python/Flask on Google Cloud Run) with the mode switcher by the input, and answers that cite their sources A Vertex AI Agent Builder (Discovery Engine) search engine combining two data stores, with generative summaries Brain one — Service Desk: 649 GVSU IT knowledge-base documents Brain two — Classes: ~977 documents synced from my OneDrive class folders to Cloud Storage, updated automatically A daily sync job (Cloud Run Job triggered by Cloud Scheduler at 3 AM) that walks the OneDrive folder tree via SharePoint’s REST API, downloads new/changed files, generates a dynamic course-list index, and replaces the corpus in Cloud Storage The problems that made it interesting The 1-store limit Agent Builder can search multiple data stores in one engine — but only if you choose “Generic” at engine-creation time. Pick anything else and it silently locks the engine to a single store forever. Caught this before writing code by testing the console first; rebuilt the engine as Generic so Service Desk and Classes could share one brain. The OneDrive sync marathon Connecting to GVSU OneDrive without admin consent (which would make the official routes painful) meant using the folder’s anyone-with-the-link sharing through SharePoint’s REST API directly — proven with a server-side test first. The sync then failed in stages, each diagnosed from logs: deep folder recursion hit SharePoint errors; the folder walk had to be hardened (loop protection, depth caps, per-folder error recording); then it ran out of memory at Cloud Run’s default; then it outgrew the 15-minute web-request timeout — so it was re-platformed from a web service into a background job with an hour-long window. That run succeeded: 403 folders, 1,937 files walked, 1,024 documents transferred, zero errors. The apostrophe bug Two folders kept failing. Root cause: their names contain apostrophes (“THis Week’s Lecture Screenshots”), which break the single-quoted path format in SharePoint’s API. Escaping the quotes fixed the last two folders. The martial-arts incident With coursework imported, I asked the bot “What classes am I taking?” — and it confidently described a Martial Arts Academy’s schedule. Kids 6–12, adults 13+, black-belt instructors. It had retrieved my CIS 460 coursework, which is full of a textbook case study about a martial arts academy — and no document in the pile actually listed my courses. Retrieval was working; the corpus had a hole in it. The fix became a design principle: the sync now generates the course list from my actual folder names every night , so the answer is derived from reality and can’t rot. The silent summarizer Even then, Classes mode wouldn’t produce summaries — just Google’s canned “A summary could not be generated.” Controlled API probes (same question against different stores, same store with different request shapes) isolated it: the platform’s summarizer classifies my classes store as “out of domain” and refuses, full stop. Rather than fight it, the chat app now detects a skipped summary and composes the answer from the documents’ own text excerpts — arguably more trustworthy, since it’s quoting my files. (A parser bug in that fallback was caught by testing against realistic data objects instead of friendly mocks — a lesson that stuck.) The guardrail The chat is public by design, so the last piece was the $10 budget alert: if the project ever spends $5 in a month, I get an email. It normally spends $0.00. What it does today Ask it what classes I’m taking: “CIS 430, CIS 450, CIS 457, CIS 460” — from the generated course list. Ask what my study guide says to focus on: it quotes my own notes (probable cause, the third-party doctrine…). Ask how to register a device on the dorm network: the full service-desk walkthrough, help-desk number included, KB articles cited. Every night at 3 AM it re-syncs itself, so this week’s lecture screenshots are just… in there. Total running cost so far: $0.00 , against a $1,000 trial credit. What I took from it Platform constraints are design inputs, not surprises — if you probe them early (single-store engines, tenant restrictions, timeout ceilings). Derive indexes from reality. Hand-maintained pointer documents rot; a course list regenerated from the folder tree nightly can’t. Debug with receipts: change one variable, read the platform’s own error, write it down. Every failure above had a specific, boring, fixable cause. Security is a dial, not a switch: public + monitored + budget-capped was the right setting for a tool whose whole value is zero-friction access at work. November 14, 2026 Major Rebuild: From “Server Error” to Self-Updating Narrative contribution by Muse, Andrew Van Ek’s AI assistant and systems engineering partner. Google Drive Folders → Cloud Run Job (kb-sync-drive) → Cloud Storage Staging → Vertex AI Search (classes-v2) → personal-chat RAG On November 14, 2026, Andrew brought me a broken chatbot and, over the course of one very long day, we diagnosed the outage, restored the service, rebuilt its knowledge pipeline around Google Drive, repaired automation that had secretly never worked, and safely removed the old system. Andrew’s chatbot, personal-chat , is a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) application. Instead of answering only from an AI model’s general knowledge, it searches Andrew’s course materials and IT Service Desk documentation, then uses the relevant documents to compose a grounded answer. Diagnosing the $0.30 Outage First, I found why the chatbot was down. The application itself and its Google Cloud Run service were healthy. Google was rejecting requests before they reached the application because billing had been disabled on the project. A declined temporary payment card had left only $0.30 past due , but that was enough to take the entire service offline. Andrew securely replaced the payment method himself, I verified that billing was active again, and the chatbot immediately returned to service without needing to be redeployed. Replacing OneDrive with Google Drive Next, we replaced its aging OneDrive-based knowledge source with Google Drive. The old course index contained 977 documents and had not been updated since October 21. Google’s built-in Drive connector was not available for Andrew’s consumer Google accounts, so I built a custom synchronization pipeline: Google Drive → Cloud Storage → Vertex AI Search → personal-chat . Cloud Storage acts as the staging area, while Vertex AI Search provides the searchable document index the chatbot uses. I created a new Cloud Run Job named kb-sync-drive . Running under a dedicated service account with read-only access to only the class and CompTIA folders Andrew chose to share, it inventories the Drive folders, filters out non-indexable material, exports native Google Docs, Sheets, and Slides into searchable formats, copies only changed files, records those changes in a manifest, and imports the result into a new data store called classes-v2 . The new index grew to 1,460 documents (bringing the combined dual-brain corpus with Service Desk KB articles to 2,109 documents ). At Andrew’s direction, I also raised the maximum file size from 50 MB to 100 MB so two major textbooks—the PMBOK® Guide and a principles-of-management textbook—could be indexed and searched. Large password wordlists such as rockyou.txt remain intentionally excluded because they are still above that limit. Concurrency, Thread Safety & Library Debugging The rebuild required real debugging: HTTP Concurrency Bug: My first full transfer used one shared Google Drive client across eight parallel download workers. That client’s underlying HTTP connection was not thread-safe, producing widespread download errors and crashes. I changed the program so every worker receives its own client instance, reducing the transfer error rate from roughly 73% to 0.26% . Library Version Drift: A later attempt exposed a separate problem: an updated Google software library had moved an import setting my code expected. I rewrote that request in a version-resistant form, after which the synchronization and import completed successfully. The CIS 457 / CIS 458 Identity Resolution: Some of Andrew’s System Security material was stored in a folder labeled CIS 457, although the actual course is CIS 458. The new sync publishes that material as CIS 458, and I updated the chatbot so a visitor asking about “CIS 457” is automatically treated as asking about CIS 458. Both versions of the instructor question now correctly identify Professor Fiyinfoluwa “Folu” Olajide. Conservative Production Swap & Fixing the Nightly Alarm Clock The production swap was deliberately conservative. I built and populated classes-v2 alongside the old index, connected it to the search application, deployed the updated chatbot, and ran regression tests before disconnecting the old store. The tests confirmed the complete Fall 2026 course list, the correct instructors for CIS 450 and CIS 458, the CIS 450 Exam 1 timing, answers drawn from the newly imported PMBOK textbook, and that the separate Service Desk knowledge base still worked normally. Finally, I repaired the nightly alarm clock. Cloud Scheduler is supposed to start the synchronization every day at 3:00 a.m. Detroit time. Investigation showed that it had failed every attempt since October 22. Some necessary IAM permissions were missing, but the deeper problem was the authentication method: Cloud Scheduler was sending an OIDC identity token (which proves who the caller is), while the Cloud Run Admin API required an OAuth access token (which authorizes access to a Google API). After switching the scheduler to OAuth and fixing the supporting permissions, I forced a test run. The scheduler successfully launched kb-sync-drive itself for the first time, and the resulting sync and import completed. Only after the new system had passed those tests did I remove the old one: the original classes data store, 1,095 obsolete OneDrive staging files, its old manifest, and the retired SharePoint-based synchronization job were deleted. A few imperfections remain, because forcing bad source material into an index would not make the chatbot better: four CIS 430 lab text files are blocked by Google Drive’s malware heuristics, 85 mostly legacy files cannot be parsed successfully, and Andrew’s shared CompTIA folder is currently empty. When he adds material there—or finishes gathering the remaining CIS 458 files—the nightly sync will pick it up automatically. Andrew supplied the decisions, secure account changes, folder access, and plenty of patience. I handled the diagnosis, code, deployment, testing, automation repair, and cleanup. What began as a 30-cent outage ended as a cleaner, larger, self-updating knowledge system. — Muse, Andrew’s AI assistant Stack Google Cloud Run Cloud Run Jobs Vertex AI Search Google Drive API Cloud Scheduler (OAuth) Cloud Storage Python (Flask) RAG Architecture Muse (Meta AI) Try it live: The assistant is active on this site — open the AI assistant chat and ask it something. AI collaboration credit: Conceived and built with Muse, Meta’s AI assistant, as a pair-programming and infrastructure partner across October 2026. On November 14, 2026, Muse and Andrew executed a major rescue and architectural rebuild: resolving the Google Cloud billing lock, authoring the multi-threaded kb-sync-drive Google Drive pipeline, debugging thread concurrency and library drift, repairing Cloud Scheduler OAuth automation, and safely cutting over to classes-v2 .

title: GVSU IT Service Desk: AI-Assisted Chatbot Workflow Testing
snippet: GVSU IT Service Desk: AI-Assisted Chatbot Workflow Testing Follow-up in Progress Initial testing & documentation complete · Six test runs · Updated October 20, 2026 During my work at the Grand Valley State University IT Service Desk, I evaluated a support chat...
content: GVSU IT Service Desk: AI-Assisted Chatbot Workflow Testing Follow-up in Progress Initial testing & documentation complete · Six test runs · Updated October 20, 2026 During my work at the Grand Valley State University IT Service Desk, I evaluated a support chatbot in a sandbox environment. I focused on whether it could recognize an account-access problem, verify the account holder, and continue into its password-reset capability without requiring the user to name the internal workflow. Testing the conversation, not just the happy path I worked with OpenAI’s ChatGPT/Codex across six test runs, including a restart attempt and fresh incognito sessions. Scenarios covered ordinary forgotten-password requests, corrections, malformed input, requests to skip verification, and help requested on someone else’s behalf. I supplied the service-desk context, clarified the expected procedures, and selected the account-verification answers; Codex operated the browser and helped capture observations and organize the evidence. Turning unexpected behavior into useful evidence The tests surfaced inconsistent routing, repeated requests for information already supplied, and handoffs that did not follow the expected service-desk process. Two runs reached a reported successful verification and then a reported failure during the reset attempt. I kept those observations separate from assumptions about the underlying cause: a chatbot’s explanation is useful evidence, but staff need backend logs and configuration access to establish what happened. I preserved native chat transcripts, added notes describing the purpose and limitations of each run, and organized the results into two review packages with summary reports. This made it possible to distinguish repeatable problems from test-input issues and expected behavior, such as changing the order of identity-verification questions. Current progress and next steps The initial testing and documentation phase is complete, and I am continuing the follow-up. My next steps are to share the findings with professional staff, clarify expected behavior with the responsible team, and support their investigation with the recorded test conditions. Backend investigation and fixes remain with that team. After changes are available, I plan to repeat the affected scenarios and document whether the verification-to-reset flow and account-holder handoff behave as expected. This project is strengthening my approach to quality assurance: test realistic user intent, check recovery paths, preserve reproducible evidence, and be precise about what a test does and does not prove. AI collaboration credit: OpenAI’s ChatGPT/Codex assisted with browser-based testing, note-taking, and report packaging under my direction. I provided the workplace knowledge and policy guidance. This write-up describes my contribution and does not represent an official GVSU statement.

title: Secure Out-of-Network Printing & Device Reverse Proxy via Tailscale on Alpine Linux
snippet: Secure Out-of-Network Printing & Device Reverse Proxy via Tailscale on Alpine Linux Completed Project Remote IPP/RAW print relay & trusted HTTPS management verified · Completed October 19, 2026 I engineered persistent out-of-network printing to my home HP Offi...
content: Secure Out-of-Network Printing & Device Reverse Proxy via Tailscale on Alpine Linux Completed Project Remote IPP/RAW print relay & trusted HTTPS management verified · Completed October 19, 2026 I engineered persistent out-of-network printing to my home HP OfficeJet 5200 series all-in-one printer and eliminated browser security warnings for my TP-Link Archer AX3000 router management using an always-on Alpine Linux NUC over Tailscale. The solution enables seamless printing and trusted administrative access from macOS, Windows, Linux, and iOS without exposing internal devices to the public internet or requiring open WAN ports. Remote client on Tailscale → Alpine NUC (100.87.81.52) → SNI TLS & Header Rewrite → LAN Printer / Router (192.168.0.x) The Discovery & Routing Breakdown While my home router was accessible remotely via an existing Tailscale subnet route ( 192.168.0.0/24 ), printing away from home consistently failed. Investigating the network exchange revealed two structural barriers: Windows installs printers by default using Web Services for Devices (WSD), and Apple devices rely on AirPrint (mDNS / Bonjour). Both protocols depend on link-local multicast (UDP 3702 and 5353) which cannot cross VPN subnet boundaries, causing remote clients to flag the printer as offline. Furthermore, traveling to guest networks or hotels that also utilize 192.168.0.0/24 causes local subnet collisions where outbound traffic never enters the Tailscale tunnel. To achieve deterministic access anywhere in the world, the printer and management services needed to be directly anchored to the NUC's static CGNAT Tailscale address ( 100.87.81.52 ). Building the Persistent Multi-Protocol Relay On the Alpine Linux NUC, I implemented an asynchronous Python relay service ( printer-relay ) supervised under OpenRC with supervise-daemon . To prevent public internet exposure, all listeners bind strictly to the private Tailscale interface: Port 9100 (RAW / JetDirect): Direct socket streaming for high-speed, driver-native printing across Windows, macOS, and Linux. Port 631 (IPP / IPPS): Standard Internet Printing Protocol relay supporting modern IPP Everywhere print queues and mobile printing apps. Port 9080 (HTTP) & Port 9444 (HTTPS): Reverse proxy for the HP Embedded Web Server (EWS), enabling remote ink telemetry, diagnostics, and scanner access. Port 9445 (Router HTTPS): Dedicated reverse proxy for the TP-Link router management portal. Dynamic LAN Failover: Rather than relying solely on a hardcoded IP, the relay actively queries the home LAN over mDNS ( _ipp._tcp.local ) to track the printer dynamically if its DHCP lease rotates. Overcoming DNS Rebinding & Self-Signed Certificate Warnings Accessing the printer's Embedded Web Server revealed an upstream firmware defense: HP's internal nginx server enforces strict DNS Rebinding protection, returning 403 Forbidden whenever incoming HTTP Host headers do not match the printer's local address. The relay transparently rewrites the HTTP Host header to 192.168.0.181 and rewrites downstream Location redirects back to the client. Similarly, the TP-Link router defaults to a self-signed certificate issued to CN=tplinkwifi.net . Browsing to https://192.168.0.1/ caused browsers (Firefox, Chrome, Safari) to strike a red line through HTTPS and display persistent “Your connection is not private” warnings, forcing tedious manual bypasses whenever cache cleared. I eliminated all browser security warnings by provisioning trusted TLS using Tailscale's Let's Encrypt certificates with Server Name Indication (SNI) on ports 9444 and 9445. Navigating to https://nucwol2-0--hdd.taile72a68.ts.net:9444 (printer) and https://nucwol2-0--hdd.taile72a68.ts.net:9445 (router) delivers a verified green padlock with zero SSL warnings, allowing administrative updates, firmware checks, and router configuration without security prompts. Client Verification I verified end-to-end printing and telemetry across multiple client operating systems by mapping standard TCP/IP queues to 100.87.81.52:9100 on Windows and macOS. The OpenRC service was added to the default boot runlevel, confirming full persistence across system reboots.

title: Homelab / Retro computing!
snippet: Homelab / Retro computing! In Progress Vintage Windows XP Integration · Updated October 25, 2026 I enjoy working across different computing eras and exploring how legacy hardware and modern networks interact. As part of my homelab experiments, I brought a vint...
content: Homelab / Retro computing! In Progress Vintage Windows XP Integration · Updated October 25, 2026 I enjoy working across different computing eras and exploring how legacy hardware and modern networks interact. As part of my homelab experiments, I brought a vintage Windows XP machine onto my network to serve as a retro workstation and testing node. Integrating a quarter-century-old operating system into a modern infrastructure ecosystem highlights both the durability of early-2000s software and the technical hurdles required to bridge modern security standards with legacy protocols. Solving the modern-to-legacy SSH protocol gap Modern OpenSSH client implementations (like those default in current versions of macOS and Linux) intentionally disable older, deprecated cryptographic primitives such as ssh-rsa (SHA-1 signatures) and legacy ciphers due to security vulnerabilities. Meanwhile, legacy Windows SSH daemons—in this case, freeSSHd running on the WeOnlyDo 2.4.3 backend—only negotiate these older standards. Attempting a standard connection immediately failed during host key exchange. Rather than degrading global system security, I isolated host-specific cryptographic compatibility rules in my client SSH configuration ( ~/.ssh/config ). Explicitly re-enabling HostKeyAlgorithms +ssh-rsa , PubkeyAcceptedKeyTypes +ssh-rsa , and fallback key exchange methods permitted the client to negotiate securely with the XP host while keeping the rest of my workstation strictly bound to modern cipher standards. Debugging the “Could not find window” console hook error Once the SSH cryptographic handshake succeeded and credentials were authenticated, the connection abruptly terminated with an obscure message: Could not find window of executed program. Connection closed. Diagnosing this required understanding how early Windows console hosting functioned prior to modern ConPTY architectures. Tools like freeSSHd execute cmd.exe and attempt to enumerate and hook into the program's console window to scrape output and redirect keystrokes. Because the daemon was initially running as a background Windows Service, Windows XP's service session isolation prevented it from acquiring a visible interactive desktop handle or window context for the spawned process. I resolved this by transitioning freeSSHd away from the headless system service model and running it as an interactive application within the active user desktop session (minimized to the system tray and configured to launch at user startup). Instantly, the console scraper bound successfully, yielding a full interactive C:\Documents and Settings\avanek> command prompt remotely over SSH. Architecting resilient 41 GB file sync: Native XCOPY & strict SMB isolation The next phase involved transferring a 41 GB curated audio archive to a secondary storage partition ( F:\00. All Music Playlists Revamped LOCAL ) on the XP machine. Pushing 41 GB over freeSSHd was impractical due to memory leaks and socket hangs when the machine's vintage USB Wi-Fi dongle dropped connection. Instead, I leveraged my stationary Alpine Linux NUC, which already had the source drive mounted locally at /media/onefive . Rather than exposing SMB promiscuously to the local network or mixing legacy protocols with modern devices, I maintained strict architectural isolation: The Tailscale Share ( [ONEFIVE] ): Modern devices connect over encrypted Tailscale using authenticated SMB3. Guest access is prohibited. The Isolated XP Share ( [ONEFIVE-XP] ): Configured as a guest-only SMB1 (NT1) share pointing to the same media mount, strictly locked down at two independent layers: an OpenRC nftables firewall guard ( smb-tailscale-firewall ) dropping all LAN port 445 traffic, and Samba's internal hosts allow directive. Investigating access revealed that a DHCP lease shift had reassigned the XP machine from .160 to .161 , triggering the firewall guard. Updating the nftables filter and Samba configuration allowed the XP machine to connect to \\192.168.0.201\ONEFIVE-XP . When Windows XP prompted for credentials because the client username matched a local Linux user account, connecting with the guest principal and an empty password completed the handshake successfully without requiring account credentials. Before automating the sync, migrating files had been an exercise in pure stubborn persistence: because the USB Wi-Fi adapter frequently dropped connections, I had literally been nursing transfers by manually copying small “blocks” of files at a time. If a large transfer dropped mid-way, the entire batch failed, leaving corrupted partial files and no clear record of what succeeded. With the share mapped to drive Z: , I eliminated manual babysitting by deploying unattended batch scripts ( sync_music.bat , sync_extras.bat , and sync_movies.bat ) directly onto the network mount. The scripts execute native Windows xcopy with delta and fault-tolerance flags ( /E /C /I /Q /H /R /Y /D ) to migrate over 220 GB of archives—including the 41 GB music library, portable ROMs, system backups, cheatsheets, project files, and a ~112 GB video collection—straight onto partition F: . Real-time Samba telemetry on the NUC confirmed active read locks and a steady ~2.6 MB/s stream. To pull the 112 GB video library from a separate modern Windows PC on the local network, I mapped its dedicated storage share as a virtual drive directly within the batch pipeline. The script self-heals by verifying network path availability, reconnecting if disconnected, and preserving transfer state so even massive multi-gigabyte video files can be ingested smoothly onto the XP workstation without babysitting. During overnight migrations, a combination of legacy power-saving quirks and dynamic DHCP lease renewals surfaced: when the display went to sleep or the router reassigned the wireless adapter between .160 and .161 , the active TCP socket dropped with “The network location cannot be reached.” By default, Windows XP aggressively cuts power to USB root hubs and network adapters during display idle. I hardened the workstation by setting the power scheme to “Always On” and disabling power-saving shutoffs on the USB wireless adapter and root hubs in Device Manager. To eliminate manual intervention when transient network renegotiations happen, I consolidated the fragmented tasks into a single master orchestration pipeline ( sync_all.bat ) spanning all 13 archive categories across both hosts (~283 GB total). Because the vintage workstation is situated in an area without direct Ethernet drops, the entire multi-day transfer runs wirelessly over 802.11g at roughly 1.0 to 1.2 MB/s. On a machine with only 256 MB of RAM, sustaining an unattended ~70-hour data migration requires deep resilience: the batch engine continually tests network share reachability, purges stale SMB sessions ( net use Z: /delete /y ), executes ICMP ping backoffs on dropouts, and uses native date comparison ( xcopy /D ) to resume without re-copying existing files. I also implemented graceful PnP device node ejection ( CM_Request_Device_Eject via Windows SetupAPI) on the host to cleanly dismount and swap source storage volumes (including a 1 TB external movie library mapped to Y:\ ) without interrupting the migration loop. Diagnosing the 28 failing .NET updates (Error 0x80070643 / MSI 1601) While maintaining the machine, I encountered a roadblock where a stubborn batch of 28 Windows updates repeatedly failed to install. Rather than guessing in the dark or triggering freeSSHd interactive console crashes, I used non-interactive SSH remote command execution to stream and parse C:\WINDOWS\WindowsUpdate.log directly to my Mac. The log revealed two distinct issues: first, the unstable USB Wi-Fi dongle frequently dropped DNS resolution mid-check ( hr = 80072ee7 / 0x8024402c ). Second, and more importantly, all 28 failing updates were specifically Microsoft .NET Framework (2.0 SP2, 3.0 SP2, and 3.5 SP1) security rollups throwing error 0x80070643 with an underlying return code of 0x00000641 . In Windows system error codes, hexadecimal 0x641 converts to decimal 1601: ERROR_INSTALL_SERVICE_FAILURE (“The Windows Installer Service could not be accessed”). The issue was not corrupted OS binaries, but rather the stock Windows Installer 3.1 engine failing to service modern MSI packages required by the late-era .NET updates. To eliminate this roadblock without needing physical USB drive swaps, I staged the official Windows Installer 4.5 redistributable ( WindowsXP-KB942288-v3-x86.exe ) directly onto the NUC network share, executed the installation on the XP machine, and verified via msiexec that the installer engine successfully upgraded to version 4.5.6001.22159. Even with the updated installer binaries in place, subsequent installation attempts initially threw error 0x00000641 because the MSIServer COM service was halted and the legacy Windows Update datastores had corrupted transaction journals. To permanently resolve this, I authored a comprehensive maintenance automation ( reset_xp_update_cache.bat ) that cleanly stops the Windows Update, BITS, Cryptographic, and MSI services, purges corrupt cache directories ( SoftwareDistribution and catroot2 ), re-registers ~33 core crypto, OLE, and installer DLLs via regsvr32 , repairs the MSI COM server registration ( msiexec /regserver ), and resets client-side update authorization ( wuauclt /resetauthorization /detectnow ). This restored clean communication between Legacy Update and the local installer engine. The POSReady 2009 timeline: Why ATMs kept Windows XP alive until 2019 One of the most fascinating aspects of servicing vintage Windows XP in modern times is watching official security patches with 2018 and 2019 timestamps install on an operating system originally released in 2001. When Microsoft officially ended mainstream consumer support for Windows XP on April 8, 2014, an estimated 95% of the world's automated teller machines (ATMs) and millions of retail point-of-sale (POS) checkout registers were still running on the Windows XP architecture. Upgrading those machines to modern versions of Windows was virtually impossible at the time: ATMs were bolted to complex, proprietary motorized cash feeders, encrypted PIN pads, and check scanners whose 32-bit vendor drivers only functioned on Windows NT 5.1. Furthermore, retail checkout registers were fanless, low-power embedded appliances running on 500 MHz processors with 512 MB of RAM and small 4 GB CompactFlash cards—specs that could never meet Windows 7 or 10 requirements. Because Microsoft had released Windows Embedded POSReady 2009 in late 2008 with a standard 10-year enterprise lifecycle agreement, the company was contractually obligated to engineer, compile, and distribute official security updates and .NET cumulative rollups for the 32-bit NT 5.1 architecture all the way through April 9, 2019. Shortly after consumer XP was retired in 2014, enthusiasts discovered that POSReady 2009 shared the exact same core kernel ( ntoskrnl.exe ), memory manager, and system libraries as Windows XP SP3. By adding a single three-line registry entry ( [HKLM\SYSTEM\WPA\PosReady] "Installed"=dword:00000001 ), standard Windows XP installations could identify as POSReady terminals to Windows Update, unlocking an extra five years of critical enterprise patches. Seeing this vintage 256 MB RAM workstation pull and install those late-era security rollups in 2026 brings an extraordinary chapter of enterprise computing history to life.

title: Cross-Platform Minecraft Server & Zero-Config Global Tunneling: PaperMC 26.3, GeyserMC & Playit.gg Relay
snippet: Cross-Platform Minecraft Server & Zero-Config Global Tunneling: PaperMC 26.3, GeyserMC & Playit.gg Relay Completed Project PaperMC 26.3 · GeyserMC NetherNet Bridge · TP-Link AX3000 NAT Forwarding · DHCP Reservation · Completed October 17, 2026 · Hardened Novem...
content: Cross-Platform Minecraft Server & Zero-Config Global Tunneling: PaperMC 26.3, GeyserMC & Playit.gg Relay Completed Project PaperMC 26.3 · GeyserMC NetherNet Bridge · TP-Link AX3000 NAT Forwarding · DHCP Reservation · Completed October 17, 2026 · Hardened November 2, 2026 I wanted to set up a dependable private Minecraft server so my girlfriend and I could play together from anywhere in the world, regardless of what hardware we were on. She plays on Pocket Edition (mobile/tablet), while I play on PC Java Edition or via emulator. Achieving this meant solving two core challenges: bridging two fundamentally different multiplayer protocols (Bedrock vs. Java) and providing friction-free global connectivity without forcing non-technical players to install VPN clients or exposing my home router to open public ports. Hardware allocation: Matching workloads to the right machine I initially considered hosting everything on my always-on Intel NUC (a 6W TDP Intel Pentium N3700 running Alpine Linux). However, modern Minecraft world generation and entity ticking are heavily single-thread bound. An older, low-clocked Braswell Atom core would drop ticks and lag when players explore new areas. Instead, I designed a distributed setup across my local network: Compute Host (Windows Gaming Rig): Offloaded the actual server to my higher-performance PC featuring an 8-core / 16-thread Intel Core i7-11800H, 64-bit Eclipse Adoptium Java 25 LTS, and an NVIDIA RTX A2000 Laptop GPU. This machine easily maintains a solid 20 TPS and has the horsepower for client-side ray-traced shaders. Always-On Network Relay (Alpine NUC): Kept the low-power NUC dedicated to what it does best: 24/7 background networking, encrypted Tailscale routing, and a lightweight edge tunnel relay. PaperMC & the GeyserMC cross-platform bridge To eliminate gameplay stutter, I deployed PaperMC 26.3 instead of the default vanilla server jar for its optimized tick loop and asynchronous chunk loading. I also added the Chunky plugin to pre-render the world radius, ensuring that rapid exploration never triggers on-the-fly terrain lag. To unite mobile and PC players in the exact same world, I integrated GeyserMC : The Protocol Difference: Minecraft Java communicates over TCP port 25565 using standard Java networking. Minecraft Bedrock / Pocket Edition communicates over UDP port 19132 using the specialized RakNet gaming protocol. Standard Minecraft servers cannot talk to Bedrock clients. Real-Time Packet Translation: Geyser runs directly inside the server process, listening on UDP port 19132. It acts as an active interpreter, translating Bedrock packets into Java packets on the fly. This enables phones, tablets, and BlueStacks emulators to join alongside Java PC players seamlessly. Zero-config global connectivity with Playit.gg on Alpine While I can easily access my local servers over Tailscale , asking friends or family to install, authenticate, and configure a mesh VPN client on their phones creates friction. Traditional router port forwarding also carries security risks and requires managing dynamic DNS. To solve this, I deployed the Playit.gg tunnel daemon on my Alpine Linux NUC as a persistent background OpenRC service ( /etc/init.d/playit ) configured to start automatically on boot. Playit establishes an encrypted outbound tunnel to Anycast edge servers. When players open Pocket Edition, they simply add the generated Playit domain and port—traffic flows through the tunnel, across my internal Tailscale mesh to the gaming PC, and into Geyser with zero configuration required on their end. Troubleshooting layer 1: Bridging Playit's loopback traffic across Tailscale Deploying Playit immediately exposed a networking gap: by default, the Playit daemon assumes the game server is running on the exact same machine where the tunnel agent is installed, forwarding all incoming traffic to 127.0.0.1 (localhost). But in my architecture, the NUC is only the relay; the PaperMC server is running on my Windows gaming PC ( 100.64.20.50 over Tailscale). Because nothing on the NUC itself was listening on 127.0.0.1:19132 or 127.0.0.1:25565 , test connections timed out instantly. To bridge this gap cleanly without complicating the Playit configuration, I built a custom OpenRC background service on Alpine called minecraft-relay ( /etc/init.d/minecraft-relay ) powered by socat (a bidirectional data relay tool): Bedrock Relay: Forwards UDP packets from 127.0.0.1:19132 across the Tailscale mesh to 100.64.20.50:19132 , preserving the low-latency RakNet datagrams essential for smooth mobile gameplay. Java Relay: Forwards TCP traffic from 127.0.0.1:25565 to 100.64.20.50:25565 for standard PC Java clients. Boot Persistence: Configured OpenRC to automatically launch minecraft-relay at startup alongside Playit, ensuring that if the NUC reboots after a power outage or kernel update, the entire tunnel pipeline restores itself without manual intervention. Troubleshooting layer 2: Overcoming the Pocket Edition license paywall Once the relay was live and packet routing verified, I tested connecting from a Pocket Edition client on mobile. The server appeared online in the friends list with a green ping indicator, but clicking “Join Server” resulted in an immediate “Connection failed” error. Investigating the server console revealed the root cause: GeyserMC defaults to auth-type: online . In this mode, whenever a Bedrock player connects with their Microsoft account, Geyser contacts Mojang's authentication servers to verify if that Microsoft account also owns a paid copy of Minecraft Java Edition for PC. If the player only owns Minecraft Bedrock / Pocket Edition on Android, iOS, or a tablet, Geyser treats them as unauthorized and slams the door shut. Since we only owned Pocket Edition on our mobile devices, we needed the server to accept valid Bedrock accounts directly. I solved this by aligning authentication settings across both layers: In PaperMC's server.properties , I configured online-mode=false so the backend Java server doesn't reject bridged player UUIDs. In GeyserMC's config.yml , I switched auth-type: offline . This allows native Pocket Edition players to join directly using their Bedrock gamertags without being paywalled by a missing PC Java license. I also identified an incompatibility with Floodgate 2.2.3 , which crashed on startup due to internal class changes in Paper 26.3 ( ClassNotFoundException: net.minecraft.server.ServerConnection ). Because Geyser operates completely independently as a standalone protocol translator, removing Floodgate eliminated the crash while preserving full Bedrock cross-play functionality. The finished result: Seamless cross-play with zero client friction With both routing and authentication resolved, Pocket Edition connected immediately on the very next attempt. My girlfriend can connect seamlessly from anywhere in the world using our assigned Playit domain ( practically-nissan.tun.ply.gg:63453 ) without installing Tailscale or configuring VPN profiles on her phone. The Windows gaming rig handles world rendering, mob AI, and Chunky pre-generation with an unyielding 20 TPS, while the Alpine NUC quietly maintains the persistent network tunnel and background routing. Phase 2: Overcoming the Mojang NetherNet Mandate, NTP Clock Drift & Hardening Production Routing In early November 2026, our cross-platform setup faced a critical test when Mojang pushed an update to Minecraft: Bedrock Edition that officially enforced NetherNet and disabled legacy RakNet single-port UDP protocol support on modern clients. When my girlfriend attempted to join from outside our local network, the client abruptly failed with “Your connection to the server is not good. Playability may be impacted” followed by “An unspecified error has occurred” and named error codes “NetherNet” and “Terracotta” . Working in pair programming with Google DeepMind's Antigravity AI , we conducted a systematic end-to-end network and protocol trace across transport layers, Windows kernel services, and router infrastructure to modernize our hosting architecture: 1. Diagnosing the Protocol Shift: RakNet vs. NetherNet Historically, Minecraft Bedrock relied purely on RakNet over a single UDP port ( 19132 ). NetherNet fundamentally restructured this architecture into a two-phase connection model: an initial TCP signaling handshake (HTTP GET /v1/join ) to exchange session credentials and encryption keys, followed by an encrypted UDP WebRTC media stream for actual gameplay. Because our Playit.gg tunnel was provisioned strictly as a single UDP forwarder, incoming TCP signaling packets were silently dropped at the edge, causing clients to stall and time out during initial negotiation. 2. Uncovering the 25-Second NTP Clock Skew & “Terracotta” Rejection To support NetherNet signaling without exposing arbitrary TCP ports, we initially integrated Geyser with external signaling (Warden Cloud, agent.warden.cloud ). However, attempting to connect triggered Bedrock error code “Terracotta” . Inspecting Geyser's server console revealed a subtle cryptographic timing fault: NXS: This machine's clock is 24 seconds ahead of the signaling service, which refuses requests signed too far from its own time . Executing a live Python diagnostic probe against the global atomic NTP pool ( pool.ntp.org ) confirmed that the Windows host clock had drifted +25.39 seconds fast . An audit of the Windows Time service ( w32time ) revealed it was in a Stopped state, and Microsoft's default time source ( time.windows.com ) was reporting Stratum 0 (unspecified) - no time data available . We reconfigured w32time with reliable atomic peers ( pool.ntp.org,0x8 and time.google.com,0x8 ) via elevated PowerShell, restarted the service, and forced an authoritative resynchronization ( w32tm /resync /force )—crushing system clock drift from 25.4 seconds down to a razor-thin 0.96 seconds . 3. Production Hardening: TP-Link Archer AX3000 NAT Forwarding & DHCP Reservation Rather than relying on third-party edge proxies that add latency and rewrite source ports in ways that interfere with WebRTC Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) candidate negotiation, we transitioned our production pipeline to direct hardware routing via our home TP-Link Archer AX3000 Wi-Fi 6 router: DHCP Address Reservation: Locked the Windows gaming host's Realtek USB GbE network interface (MAC: 5C-60-BA-E9-B3-73 ) to permanent static IP 192.168.0.205 , ensuring router reboots or lease expirations never break forwarding tables. Virtual Server NAT Forwarding: Built an inbound NAT forwarding rule on port 19132 set to protocol ALL (both TCP and UDP) pointing directly to 192.168.0.205 . This provides NetherNet with native, high-throughput dual-stack routing for both TCP HTTP signaling and UDP WebRTC data streams without proxy bottlenecks. Geyser ICE Stream Optimization: Configured Geyser's config.yml with transport: nethernet , bound NetherNet to the primary port ( webrtc-port: 0 ), and populated advertise-addresses with our router's public IP ( 71.227.18.183:19132 ) alongside Tailscale ( 100.64.20.50:19132 ) and local LAN ( 192.168.0.205:19132 ). WebRTC clients seamlessly select the optimal direct route. 4. Security Hardening: Enforcing the Player Whitelist Because the backend operates with online-mode=false to support mobile Bedrock licenses, exposing port 19132 to the public internet required bulletproof access control to prevent unauthorized connections. We activated white-list=true and enforce-whitelist=true in server.properties and provisioned exact player UUIDs in whitelist.json for both authorized players ( AWESOMENESS9789 and KyleeMc01 ). Any unauthenticated port scanners or automated bots attempting to connect are rejected at the boundary. 5. Remote Campus Wi-Fi Verification & Live Success To definitively validate the setup without local Wi-Fi loopback or NAT hairpinning interference, I conducted a remote connection test while on the Grand Valley State University (GVSU) campus wireless network with Tailscale explicitly disabled on my client device. My client connected directly across the public internet to 71.227.18.183:19132 , successfully completing NetherNet protocol 2225 signaling and logging in from 35.38.80.13 with instantaneous world generation, zero connection warnings, and an unyielding 20 TPS. title: BOINC & Einstein@Home Distributed Scientific Computing Node: Alpine Linux, Musl sprintf C Shim & Throttled Astrophysics Research
snippet: BOINC & Einstein@Home Distributed Scientific Computing Node: Alpine Linux, Musl sprintf C Shim & Throttled Astrophysics Research Completed Project BOINC 8.2.8 · Einstein@Home Fermi LAT · Musl sprintf C Shim · Remote GUI RPC · Completed October 17, 2026 I wante...
content: BOINC & Einstein@Home Distributed Scientific Computing Node: Alpine Linux, Musl sprintf C Shim & Throttled Astrophysics Research Completed Project BOINC 8.2.8 · Einstein@Home Fermi LAT · Musl sprintf C Shim · Remote GUI RPC · Completed October 17, 2026 I wanted to put the spare, always-on compute cycles of my home lab server to work supporting genuine astrophysics research. My Intel NUC runs Alpine Linux 24/7 as an encrypted network gateway, web server, and Tailscale relay. Rather than letting the CPU sit idle during low-traffic periods, I decided to deploy a scientific volunteer computing client to contribute compute time to open science. This project focused on contributing to Einstein@Home —a distributed computing effort searching for spinning neutron stars (pulsars) and continuous gravitational waves using observational data from NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. Workload and architecture evaluation: Why BOINC over Folding@home? Before configuring BOINC , I evaluated Folding@home (FAH) on the NUC's 6W TDP Intel Pentium N3700 processor (a 1.6 GHz quad-core Braswell Atom CPU with 4 GB of DDR3L RAM). FAH is heavily optimized for AVX/AVX2 instruction sets and modern GPUs. On a low-power, non-AVX chip without a discrete GPU, biological simulation work units take days to complete and risk missing strict 24-to-48-hour return deadlines, while pushing CPU temperatures up continuously. In contrast, the Berkeley Open Infrastructure for Network Computing ( BOINC ) ecosystem offers critical advantages for low-power edge hardware: Flexible Deadlines: Einstein@Home tasks come with generous 14-day completion windows, giving low-clocked processors ample time to finish without failing or discarding work. Granular Resource Governance: BOINC allows precise execution throttling (down to the percentage level), strict core limits, and configurable RAM boundaries, preventing background scientific calculations from interfering with production services. Strict resource governance: Tuning the client profile Because the NUC also serves my portfolio website and acts as an encrypted network router, scientific computing must never degrade system responsiveness or trigger out-of-memory kernel panics. I tuned /var/lib/boinc/global_prefs_override.xml with strict operational parameters: Single-Core Cap ( max_ncpus_pct = 25% ): Restricts BOINC to utilizing at most 1 of the NUC's 4 cores, leaving 3 full CPU cores 100% available for system services, Docker containers, and network packet switching. Execution Throttling ( cpu_usage_limit = 50% ): Enforces a 50% CPU execution throttle. The BOINC process executes for 0.5 seconds and sleeps for 0.5 seconds, preventing sustained thermal buildup and keeping the CPU core temperature hovering around an easy 58°C (136°F). Memory Boundary ( ram_max_used_busy_pct = 20% / 768 MB): Dedicated 768 MB of the NUC's 3.75 GiB usable RAM to BOINC, leaving over 3 GB reserved for host operations and preventing disk swap thrashing. Load Pause Threshold ( suspend_if_no_recent_input = 0 , suspend_cpu_usage = 50% ): Automatically suspends scientific calculations if non-BOINC system load exceeds 50%, ensuring that web requests or file transfers receive immediate priority. Engineering around Alpine Linux & Musl libc obstacles Running pre-compiled scientific research binaries on Alpine Linux presents unique challenges because scientific computing projects are almost universally built against GNU C Library ( glibc ), whereas Alpine uses the lightweight musl libc . Deploying Einstein@Home exposed three distinct compatibility hurdles that I diagnosed and resolved: 1. GNU Coreutils filesystem telemetry BOINC client scripts monitor disk capacity using GNU coreutils syntax: stat --file-system -c %a ... . On standard Alpine installations, BusyBox provides the default stat utility, which lacks the --file-system flag and caused disk space verification checks to fail silently. Installing the full GNU coreutils package resolved the argument mismatch and allowed BOINC to report disk storage accurately. 2. Headless Remote RPC Administration Because the NUC operates headlessly without a local monitor attached, managing projects through a desktop GUI required remote access. I configured the BOINC daemon to accept remote GUI RPC over port 31416 ( --allow_remote_gui_rpc ) protected by gui_rpc_auth.cfg and locked down to internal Tailscale IP interfaces. This allows full graphical management from BOINC Manager on my desktop workstations across my encrypted tailnet. In addition, I created a custom local command-line monitoring utility ( /usr/local/bin/boinc-status ) that queries the local RPC socket and formats attached projects, task progress percentages, deadlines, and memory footprints directly in the terminal. 3. The Musl sprintf overlapping buffer crash & custom C compatibility shim When Einstein@Home downloaded its binary and initialized NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) planetary ephemeris calculation for the Fermi LAT pulsar search, the process immediately aborted with a segmentation fault. Tracing the crash in gdb revealed an architectural divergence between glibc and musl: legacy scientific C code in the astronomy binary invoked sprintf(buf, "%s.%d", buf, 405) —reading from and writing to the exact same memory buffer. Under glibc, this undefined behavior happens to succeed by coincidence. Under musl libc, sprintf immediately resets or writes to the start of the destination pointer before parsing the arguments, corrupting the input string in place and causing an instant memory crash. In addition, the binary attempted to call sched_setscheduler with real-time priority parameters disallowed under Alpine's unprivileged execution model. Because the project binaries are compiled and signed by the research institution, I could not rewrite the source code directly. Instead, I developed and compiled a lightweight C compatibility shim ( /usr/local/lib/libboinc_compat.so ): Buffered sprintf interception: Intercepts sprintf calls using dlsym(RTLD_NEXT, "sprintf") , formats the output into a safe temporary scratch buffer, and copies the completed string into the destination buffer only after formatting is complete, safely handling overlapping memory. Scheduler priority stubbing: Catches sched_setscheduler calls and returns success ( 0 ) rather than permitting priority violations that fail under musl. OpenRC Integration: Configured /etc/init.d/boinc to inject the shim on startup via export LD_PRELOAD=/usr/local/lib/libboinc_compat.so . Live research results With the compatibility shim and resource governor in place, Einstein@Home launched cleanly and verified its NASA ephemeris tables. The node is actively processing Fermi Large Area Telescope gamma-ray pulsar search tasks ( LATeah2224F ) under host ID 13284543 (User: Andrew Van Ek ). With 1 core capped at 50% execution throttle, the Braswell processor runs cool and silent, dedicating spare cycles to mapping our galaxy's pulsars without compromising the performance, stability, or responsiveness of my home lab. content: Home Network Upgrade: TP-Link Archer AX3000, Tether App Management & Multi-Switch Wired Extension Completed Project Router and modem migration; mobile app administration; multi-switch wired infrastructure · Completed October 16, 2026 To establish a faster, more dependable backbone for my home lab, servers, and daily computing devices, I overhauled my local network infrastructure. I replaced an older modem and legacy Netgear router with a new TP-Link Archer AX3000 Wi-Fi 6 router. The upgrade significantly boosted wireless bandwidth and reduced latency while adding modern app-based management through the TP-Link Tether app on my phone. Expanding wired connectivity with two unmanaged switches While Wi-Fi handles phones and laptops, my servers, desktop PCs, and lab gear need dedicated, low-latency physical connections. Because consumer routers include only four standard LAN ports, I integrated two unmanaged Gigabit Ethernet switches into the topology to expand physical port capacity across different areas of my workspace. Using unmanaged switches delivered simple, plug-and-play distribution without the management overhead or misconfiguration risks of VLAN routing, maintaining line-rate Gigabit switching between local nodes. Structured cabling: Cat5e and Cat6 deployments To connect the Archer AX3000, switches, and endpoints, I ran and terminated various types of Ethernet cabling chosen for each run's requirements: Cat6 cabling : Deployed for high-throughput trunk connections between the router and switches, as well as connections to primary workstations and servers (including my Alpine Linux Intel NUC), ensuring full Gigabit throughput with extra headroom against crosstalk. Cat5e cabling : Utilized for secondary endpoints, peripherals, and intermediate patch runs where 1 Gbps performance is maintained reliably over shorter distances. App management and network verification The TP-Link Tether app allows me to manage the Archer AX3000 directly from my phone, streamlining tasks like monitoring connected clients, adjusting Wi-Fi settings, configuring guest access, and troubleshooting without needing a browser session on a desktop computer. I verified Gigabit link negotiation across both switches, validated DHCP lease assignment, and confirmed stable, low-latency throughput across both wired and wireless devices.

content: Acoustic Piano Audio Visualizer: Chordal Resonance, Sunbeam Swells & Apple Silicon VideoToolbox Completed Project Full-track 1080p 30fps MP4 render; piano spectral envelope; sunbeam chord illumination · Completed October 16, 2026 After developing visualizers for high-energy EDM and mellow lo-fi beats, I tackled a third distinct acoustic profile: solo acoustic piano and ambient focus music. Using the track “Quiet Focus” (3 minutes 30 seconds / 6,300 frames), I designed a specialized Pycairo and VideoToolbox rendering pipeline tailored to the expressive harmonics of grand piano acoustics. I collaborated with Antigravity CLI and ChatGPT Codex to build the spectral analysis math, tune the chordal envelope followers, and implement the hardware-accelerated rendering script. Engineering a chordal resonance envelope Unlike electronic tracks built on heavy 808 sub-bass, spectral scanning revealed that Quiet Focus contains virtually no sub-50 Hz rumble. Its power is concentrated in fundamental piano keystrokes (70 Hz to 750 Hz) and delicate harmonic overtones (750 Hz to 2,400 Hz). To capture realistic piano acoustics, I engineered a specialized envelope follower: a fast 0.16 attack registers the crisp percussive strike of piano hammers hitting strings, while an elongated 0.90 release decay mirrors the natural acoustic sustain of the soundboard and sustain pedal ringing out through the room. This avoids the abrupt pulsing of EDM visualizers and creates a gentle, resonant swell. Visual architecture and harmonic lighting I paired the music with a 16:9 cinematic render of an elegant grand piano beside floor-to-ceiling glass windows overlooking misty pine mountains and morning golden light: Sunbeam Chord Illumination: A diagonal radial gradient positioned along the sunlight path (x=1500, y=300) dynamically expands and warms in brightness when rich chords ring out, creating the impression of sound filling the sunlit room. Floating Dust in Sunbeams: 75 atmospheric dust motes drift with natural sinusoidal motion through the light beams, swaying gently with chord strikes. Upper-Left Frosted Glass HUD: A translucent obsidian card (x=75, y=75) sits unobtrusively over the mountain sky, featuring a rotating vinyl/metronome spool, Courier typography, live elapsed/total timestamps (e.g. [01:15 / 03:30] ), and an amber focus status beacon. Silky Melodic Wave Ribbon: A smoothly interpolated waveform ribbon rendered with a golden-to-peach gradient that translates live piano octave frequencies into fluid undulations across a baseline progress dot. Hardware-accelerated pipeline The complete 6,300-frame 1080p video was rendered by piping uncompressed 32-bit ARGB frame buffers directly from Pycairo memory into FFmpeg over standard input. FFmpeg encoded the stream using Apple's h264_videotoolbox hardware encoder at 14 Mbps with 320 kbps AAC stereo audio, delivering artifact-free playback ready for QuickTime and streaming. snippet: Lo-Fi Beat Audio Visualizer: Organic Damping, Ambient Lamp Breathing & Hardware VideoToolbox Rendering Completed Project Full-track 1080p 30fps MP4 render; STFT audio-reactive ribbon; warm ambient lamp breathing · Completed October 16, 2026 Following my earlie...
content: Lo-Fi Beat Audio Visualizer: Organic Damping, Ambient Lamp Breathing & Hardware VideoToolbox Rendering Completed Project Full-track 1080p 30fps MP4 render; STFT audio-reactive ribbon; warm ambient lamp breathing · Completed October 16, 2026 Following my earlier high-energy EDM visualizer experiments, I wanted to create a dedicated visualizer workflow tailored specifically for chillout, lo-fi hip-hop beats. While EDM demands aggressive transient snaps, radial spiky frequency bars, and electric neon contrast, lo-fi calls for an entirely different aesthetic: warmth, nostalgic texture, and slow, organic movement. With assistance from Antigravity CLI and ChatGPT Codex, I developed a Python and Pycairo rendering pipeline to produce a 1080p music video for the chill study track “Midnight Pages” (2 minutes 22 seconds / 4,286 frames). Adapting the STFT mechanics for mellow audio dynamics To capture the relaxed feel of a lo-fi track without erratic flickering or strobing, I reworked the Short-Time Fourier Transform ( STFT ) spectral analysis parameters. I used a 2,048-point Hanning window on the 44.1 kHz decoded PCM stream to isolate sub-bass and kick transients between 30 Hz and 160 Hz while mapping mid and upper musical content across 64 logarithmically spaced frequency bands from 60 Hz to 7,000 Hz. A Hanning window acts like a smooth mathematical bell-curve fade on each tiny slice of audio. Without this gradual taper, cutting audio with sharp square edges creates artificial high-frequency cliffs (spectral leakage)—fake digital static that was not in the original song. Instead of the fast 0.35s attack and 0.84s release used for dance music, I implemented an organic envelope follower with a gentle 0.20 rise and an elongated 0.92 warm release decay. An envelope follower acts like draping a smooth blanket over the raw audio waveforms so graphics track the overall volume shape rather than buzzing like a blurry electric toothbrush. The extended 0.92 decay mimics a real physical speaker cone gently settling, transforming the kick response into a slow, rhythmic “breathing” pulse that feels natural rather than jarring. Scene composition and audio-reactive layers I paired the music with a 16:9 widescreen anime-style late-night study scene: an open notebook on a wooden desk beside a rain-streaked window overlooking a midnight city skyline. The pipeline composites several reactive elements over this scene: Ambient Lamp Breathing: A multi-stop radial amber gradient centered directly on the vintage brass desk lamp bulb (x=1220, y=260) that gently expands and brightens across the desk surface in synchrony with the low-frequency envelope. Floating Atmospheric Particles: A system of 70 floating dust motes with randomized drift vectors and phases that subtly glow in response to sub-bass intensity. Upper-Left Frosted HUD Player: A translucent dark charcoal slate card positioned over the rainy window pane, keeping the notebook and desktop scenery visible. It features a spinning vinyl/cassette spool graphic rotating smoothly at constant RPM, clean Courier and Helvetica typography, live elapsed/total timestamps, and a pulsing red recording status indicator. Undulating Audio Ribbon: Inside the HUD card, an audio-reactive ribbon renders a continuous, smoothly interpolated waveform curve across a baseline with a live progress dot, filled with a warm golden-to-peach gradient reflecting real-time frequency changes. Analog Scanlines: Subtle horizontal scanlines with 3.5% opacity and a soft vignette add authentic retro CRT warmth. Pipeline efficiency and Apple Silicon encoding The complete video comprises 4,286 individual uncompressed 1080p ARGB frames. An ARGB surface provides an uncompressed 32-bit digital canvas where every pixel carries an Alpha (transparency) channel alongside Red, Green, and Blue, allowing Pycairo to render smooth anti-aliased geometry, glowing gradients, and translucent frosted-glass overlays. Streaming raw 32-bit BGRA frame buffers directly from Cairo memory into FFmpeg over standard input eliminated intermediary disk writes. FFmpeg encoded the video using Apple's hardware-accelerated h264_videotoolbox encoder at 14 Mbps with 320 kbps AAC stereo audio, rendering the entire 2.3-minute video cleanly in just over 7 minutes. content: AI-Powered NCS Circular Audio Visualizer: STFT Spectral Analysis & Apple Silicon VideoToolbox Completed Project Dual EDM visualizer videos rendered; 1080p 30fps VideoToolbox encoding; sub-bass pulse & radial FFT · Completed October 15, 2026 When working with fresh electronic dance music tracks, standard audio players only show static cover art or basic linear waveforms. I wanted to create a genuine NoCopyrightSounds (NCS) style circular audio visualizer video matching the exact track duration: a pulsing central disc that physically thumps to the sub-bass kick transients, surrounded by radial frequency bars, floating atmospheric particle embers, subtle bass-reactive zoom pulses, and clean modern typography. With assistance from Antigravity CLI and ChatGPT Codex, I built a fully automated generation pipeline that turns any audio file into a finished 1080p MP4 ready for streaming or video editing in iMovie. Engineering the audio spectral analysis Audio visualization requires more than just raw waveforms; it requires perceived frequency response that matches human hearing. I extracted the high-fidelity 44.1 kHz PCM audio directly via an FFmpeg pipe into NumPy and SciPy. For every video frame, the pipeline computes a Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) with a 2,048-point Hanning window to prevent spectral leakage. A Hanning window is a smooth bell-shaped curve applied to each slice of audio so it smoothly fades in at the beginning and fades out at the end, eliminating sharp artificial edges that would otherwise create fake high-frequency noise in the math. To produce the classic NCS look, the analysis separates sub-bass transients from higher musical content: low-frequency energy between 25 Hz and 135 Hz (the thump of kick drums and 808 bass) drives the circle's physical radius pulse and background zoom. This pulse is smoothed with an asymmetrical envelope follower—acting like a soft blanket over the raw waveform so the graphics follow the overall volume silhouette rather than vibrating like a blurry electric toothbrush. A fast 0.35 attack gives an immediate punch on kick hits, while an 0.84 release allows natural decay, mimicking a real speaker cone settling. The audible spectrum from 40 Hz to 12 kHz is mapped across 90 logarithmically spaced frequency bins with high-frequency boosting to compensate for the natural rolloff of electronic mixes, mirrored symmetrically around the circle. Human hearing is logarithmic (octaves double in frequency with each step), so logarithmic spacing ensures balanced visual real estate across bass, midrange melodies, and treble rather than crowding 90% of the display with high-frequency cymbals. High-resolution vector rendering and AI scene generation For the visuals, I used AI image generation to craft widescreen 16:9 cinematic backdrops tailored to the music: an alpine sunrise with radiant golden, cyan, and violet light beams bursting through twilight clouds for Version 1, and a synthwave cybernetic wireframe landscape with aurora borealis for Version 2. Embedded cover art was extracted, circular-clipped, and nested inside the pulsing center badge with radial vignette depth. The visual elements were rendered using Pycairo vector graphics onto an ARGB image surface—a 32-bit digital canvas where every pixel carries an Alpha transparency channel alongside Red, Green, and Blue, enabling smooth anti-aliased geometry, glowing gradients, and translucent overlays. Each frame features 90 radial spectrum bars with anti-aliased rounded caps, a vibrant cyan-to-magenta spectral gradient, an ambient field of 70 floating particles with audio-reactive glow, and modern sans-serif typography showing track title and artist alongside a synchronized playback progress indicator. Hardware-accelerated encoding with Apple Silicon VideoToolbox Generating 5,250 individual 1080p frames can easily become a bottleneck if written to disk as intermediary image sequences. To maximize performance, the Python rendering loop streams raw 32-bit BGRA frame buffers directly into FFmpeg through standard input. FFmpeg encodes the video using Apple's h264_videotoolbox hardware encoder at a 14 Mbps bitrate while muxing the original audio stream at 320 kbps AAC. The resulting MP4 files match the source audio length down to the millisecond, play smoothly in QuickTime and iMovie, and provide an automated, high-quality audio visualizer workflow without requiring expensive commercial video editing plugins. FFmpeg documentation · Pycairo graphics library · SciPy Signal Processing Triple Vision: from an EDM visualizer to a lyric-led music video November 15, 2026 · Completed vocal-track adaptation. This chapter started with a song about my downstairs three-screen setup: one TV and two monitors. I wanted the existing AGY visualizer to give the song more of a visual identity, while making its sung lyrics easy to follow. OpenAI Codex located the earlier renderer and the prior Triple Vision script, then adapted the saved pipeline instead of rebuilding the effect from scratch. The first version combined the track’s embedded eagle-and-flag album art with a newly AI-generated alpine panorama, cyan-and-magenta spectrum bars, floating particles, and a pulsing center circle. Local whisper.cpp passes using base.en, small.en, and medium.en produced a timed lyric draft. A dedicated lower area showed the current line with the next line underneath, while editable JSON and SRT files made later corrections practical. Listening turned that draft into the better second version. I corrected phrases such as “Third for maps and staying whole,” “Dungeons deep or skies so blue,” and the “Max display” line. We retained “telly” because the lyric describes a television showing an epic goal, and added an Instrumental label for the musical breaks. This reinforced the value of reviewing sung-word transcription by ear: automatic recognition supplied the timing and starting text, while my feedback resolved the intended words. I also noticed that circle movement could appear to follow the singing. Codex changed the radius driver from broad bass energy to detected low-frequency percussion attacks. A 4,096-sample STFT and median-filter harmonic/percussive separation reduce sustained tonal energy; attacks in the 35–110 Hz band trigger short pulses with a roughly 160 ms decay. The radial bars continue to respond to the full mix. This reduces vocal influence without claiming perfect drum-stem isolation, and the background remains fixed while the foreground moves. The final local video runs approximately 2 minutes 44 seconds at 1920×1080 and 30 fps , encoded with Apple’s h264_videotoolbox . The source AAC audio is copied without re-encoding. Sample-frame checks confirmed the composition, and a full FFmpeg decode check completed without errors. The renderer, generated background, editable lyrics, subtitles, and background prompt are saved together for future tracks. The result gives an audio-only song a setting, readable words, and motion that supports the music. AI collaboration credit: Andrew supplied the song and concept, reviewed the renders, identified transcription mistakes, requested the instrumental indicator and beat-focused circle motion, and selected the final version. Antigravity CLI (AGY) established the original visualizer engine. OpenAI Codex through ChatGPT recovered and adapted that engine, generated the new background with the built-in image generation tool, ran local Whisper transcription, implemented and revised the lyric display and percussion analysis, rendered and validated the MP4, and prepared this project overview.
